meta.blurb: For twenty years Charles Darwin quietly collected facts. Then a letter from Alfred Russel Wallace arrived with the same idea, and he rushed to write. Here is the book that argues nature, not a breeder, picks who survives.
meta.bible: Charles Darwin: English naturalist, born 1809, who sailed on HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836 and later lived and worked at Down House in Kent. On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection: his book, published by John Murray in London on 24 November 1859; the full title adds 'or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life'. Alfred Russel Wallace: a naturalist working in Ternate who in 1858 wrote to Darwin about the same idea. Charles Lyell and Joseph Hooker: Darwin's friends, who arranged for both men's ideas to be read at the Linnean Society in July 1858. The book has an Introduction and fourteen chapters; Darwin called it 'one long argument'. Its only picture is one Diagram of a branching tree. Key terms: Species, Variation, Domestication, Breeders, Selection, Natural Selection, Struggle for Existence, Malthus (Thomas Malthus, a writer on populations), Divergence, Instinct, Hybrids, Sterile, Fossils, Geological, Extinction, Embryos, Rudimentary, Descent, Evolved, Fantail, Pouter, Tumbler, Pigeons, Rock Pigeon, Peacock, Cuckoo, Honeybee, Hexagonal, Wallace, Tangled Bank, Galapagos, Armadillos, Sloths, Vertebrates, Naturalists, Creation, Wolves, Lyell, Hooker, Linnean, Beagle, Kent, Ternate, Murray, Mammals, Pollinate, Clover, Humble-bees, Nectar, Hereditary, Mankind. Darwin is careful and modest in the text: he lists his own difficulties and says where he does not know. This book retells the argument faithfully, adds no invented numbers or quotes, and says plainly where Darwin or later science is uncertain. Voice: clear, patient and wondering, like a good teacher who respects both Darwin and the reader. Extra facts for the full-length book: Charles Darwin was born on 12 February 1809 in Shrewsbury; he studied medicine in Edinburgh, then at Cambridge prepared to be a clergyman, and was a friend of the botanist John Stevens Henslow, who recommended him to Captain Robert FitzRoy of HMS Beagle. The Beagle left Plymouth on 27 December 1831 and reached Falmouth on 2 October 1836. Places on the voyage: Brazil, Patagonia, Chile, Valdivia, Andes, Galapagos, Tahiti, New Zealand, Australia, Keeling Islands, Cape Town. Charles Lyell wrote Principles of Geology, which Darwin read on the voyage. John Gould, a bird expert in London, told Darwin in 1837 that his Galapagos birds were a group of finches. Darwin married his cousin Emma Wedgwood on 29 January 1839; they had ten children and moved to Down House in the village of Down, Kent, in 1842; the Sandwalk was his thinking path. He spent about eight years on Barnacles. In 1844 he wrote a long private essay; Hooker was the first friend he told. He wrote to the American botanist Asa Gray in 1857. Wallace's essay reached him on 18 June 1858; his baby son Charles Waring died of scarlet fever on 28 June 1858; both men's papers were read at the Linnean Society on 1 July 1858. Darwin finished the book in about thirteen months and was at a water-cure at Ilkley when it came out; the first printing was about 1,250 copies and a second edition of 3,000 followed in January 1860. Thomas Huxley supported the book; at Oxford in June 1860 Huxley and Bishop Samuel Wilberforce argued about it at a scientific meeting (accounts of what was said differ), and Darwin was not there. Darwin died on 19 April 1882 and is buried in Westminster Abbey. Other people and places named: Linnaeus, Lamarck, Erasmus Darwin (his grandfather), Herschel, Sebright, Youatt, Bakewell, Kolreuter, Gartner, Wollaston, Madeira, Panama, Weald, Archaeopteryx, Solnhofen, Von Baer, Kentucky, Catskill, Paraguay, Surrey, Scotland, Mendel, Australia, Africa, America, Europe, Brazil. Extra key terms: Beetles, Barnacles, Tortoises, Finches, Mockingbirds, Earthquake, Rainforest, Specimens, Notebooks, Fever, Ducks, Cats, Mice, Bees, Wasps, Ants, Flies, Cockroach, Thrush, Sheep, Cattle, Horses, Donkey, Mule, Zebra, Stripes, Giraffe, Squirrel, Lingula, Trilobites, Ammonites, Glyptodon, Megatherium, Mastodon, Kangaroos, Embryo, Larva, Larvae, Caterpillar, Crustacean, Crustaceans, Cambrian, Silurian, Glacial, Alpine, Arctic, Isthmus, Colonists, Organs, Pollen, Wedges, Genes, Heredity, Inherited, Offspring, Fertile, Hybrid, Mongrels, Transitional, Neuter, Workers, Pupae.

beats.scene: A boy in Shrewsbury fills his pockets with beetles and shells beside a river
beats.summary: Charles Darwin is born in Shrewsbury in 1809 and as a boy collects beetles, shells and stones.

beats.scene: A young man hunts beetles in the fields near Cambridge with his professor
beats.summary: Darwin studies medicine and then prepares to become a clergyman, but he spends his time collecting beetles and walking with the botanist Henslow.

beats.scene: A letter arrives at a country house offering a place on a ship
beats.summary: Henslow recommends Darwin to Captain FitzRoy of the survey ship Beagle, and Darwin's uncle helps persuade his father to let him go.

beats.scene: The small ship Beagle leaves Plymouth harbour under grey skies
beats.summary: The Beagle sails from Plymouth on 27 December 1831 on a trip planned for two years; it lasts nearly five, and Darwin is often seasick.

beats.scene: Darwin walks under huge trees and bright flowers in a Brazilian rainforest
beats.summary: In the forests of Brazil, Darwin sees a crowd of living things he has never imagined.

beats.scene: Darwin digs huge old bones out of a cliff on a windy coast
beats.summary: In South America Darwin finds the bones of huge extinct animals, strangely like smaller animals still living there.

beats.scene: A forest and a stormy shore after an earthquake, with fish lying on rocks
beats.summary: In Chile in February 1835, Darwin feels an earthquake, and afterwards sees that the shore has been lifted above the sea.

beats.scene: Darwin holds a sea shell found among rocks high in the Andes mountains
beats.summary: In the Andes Darwin finds sea shells far above the sea, which fits the idea in Lyell's book that the land changes slowly over great ages.

beats.scene: Giant tortoises and dark lizards on a black volcanic shore of the Galapagos
beats.summary: In late 1835 the Beagle reaches the Galapagos Islands, where Darwin collects birds, plants, tortoises and lizards.

beats.scene: Darwin on deck looks at a ring of coral around a quiet lagoon
beats.summary: On the way home Darwin works out how coral islands form, and the Beagle reaches England on 2 October 1836 with boxes of specimens and notebooks.

beats.scene: Darwin and a bird expert bend over a table of small birds in London
beats.summary: In 1837 the bird expert John Gould tells Darwin that his Galapagos birds are all finches, yet different kinds.

beats.scene: A notebook open on a desk shows a small branching tree drawn in ink
beats.summary: In 1837 Darwin starts a secret notebook on how species might change and draws his first small tree of branching life.

beats.scene: Darwin reads by a window with a thick book open on his knee
beats.summary: In 1838 Darwin reads Thomas Malthus on how human numbers grow faster than food, and sees that the same struggle must happen in all of nature.

beats.scene: A newly married couple walks up the path of a country house garden
beats.summary: Darwin marries his cousin Emma Wedgwood in 1839, and in 1842 the family moves to Down House in Kent.

beats.scene: Darwin walks slowly along a sandy path through a small wood, thinking
beats.summary: At Down, Darwin walks every day on his thinking path, the Sandwalk, and works in short stretches because he is often ill.

beats.scene: A magnifying glass over a tiny barnacle on a laboratory table
beats.summary: For about eight years Darwin studies barnacles in great detail, which teaches him how much living things vary.

beats.scene: A husband quietly hands a sealed letter of instructions to his wife
beats.summary: In 1842 and 1844 Darwin writes out his theory in private essays and tells his wife to publish the longer one if he dies; he tells his friend Hooker first.

beats.scene: Darwin stands in a loft full of fancy pigeons with a letter beside him
beats.summary: Darwin keeps pigeons at home and writes to breeders, farmers and gardeners around the world to gather facts.

beats.scene: Two friends in a library speak seriously over a heavy book of geology
beats.summary: In 1856 Charles Lyell urges Darwin to write out his theory before someone else does, so Darwin begins a huge book called Natural Selection.

beats.scene: A man writes a long letter to a friend across the ocean
beats.summary: In 1857 Darwin explains his idea in a letter to the American botanist Asa Gray, but still does not publish.

beats.scene: A young man with a butterfly net walks through a hot tropical forest
beats.summary: Alfred Russel Wallace, a British collector who sells specimens to museums, spends about eight years in the islands of south-east Asia.

beats.scene: A sick man lies in a hut on a tropical island, thinking
beats.summary: In early 1858, ill with fever on the island of Ternate, Wallace thinks about Malthus and sees how survival could shape species; he writes it up in a few evenings.

beats.scene: Darwin sits at his desk reading a letter with a worried face
beats.summary: Darwin receives Wallace's essay on 18 June 1858 and is dismayed to find that it describes almost exactly his own theory.

beats.scene: A family stands quietly at a window in a house in mourning
beats.summary: Ten days later, on 28 June 1858, Darwin's baby son Charles Waring dies of scarlet fever, and Darwin can hardly think of his work.

beats.scene: Two men in frock coats discuss two sets of papers in a study
beats.summary: Lyell and Hooker decide to present Wallace's essay together with earlier writings by Darwin, so that both men share the credit.

beats.scene: A hall full of scientists listens as papers are read aloud
beats.summary: On 1 July 1858 both papers are read at the Linnean Society in London; neither man is there, and the audience says little.

beats.scene: A society president speaks solemnly at a lectern beneath a portrait
beats.summary: The Society's president later says the year had brought no striking discoveries, which shows how little the world saw what was coming.

beats.scene: Wallace reads a letter at a rough table in a tent in a forest
beats.summary: Wallace is delighted when he hears the news, and the two men remain friendly; Wallace later praises Darwin's work and calls his own book Darwinism.

beats.scene: Darwin at his desk writing quickly while piles of notes surround him
beats.summary: Darwin sets aside his huge book and writes a shorter one that he calls an abstract; it takes about thirteen months and grows far longer than planned.

beats.scene: A publisher and an author examine a heavy book with a long title
beats.summary: The publisher John Murray agrees to print the book, which is titled On the Origin of Species and is published on 24 November 1859.

beats.scene: An open book beside a quill, with a ship model behind it
beats.summary: The Introduction begins with the Beagle voyage and with what Darwin calls the mystery of mysteries: where new kinds of living things come from.

beats.scene: Old bones in a cliff and finches on a branch, on one page
beats.summary: Two sets of facts from the voyage stand out: the fossil animals that resemble living ones in the same place, and the way island animals differ from island to island.

beats.scene: A heavy pile of notes tied with string beside a small book
beats.summary: Darwin says he has worked on the subject for many years, that this book is only a short summary, and that he cannot give all his evidence or his sources here.

beats.scene: Wallace, a tent and a rain forest, with a printed page before him
beats.summary: Darwin tells his readers that Wallace, now studying the animals and plants of the Malay islands, has reached almost exactly the same conclusions.

beats.scene: A row of old naturalists in dark coats nod beside a shelf of jars
beats.summary: Before Darwin, most naturalists believed that each species was made separately and never changes; a few thinkers, like Lamarck and Darwin's own grandfather, had suggested otherwise.

beats.scene: A woodpecker clings to a tree trunk while a sprig of mistletoe hangs nearby
beats.summary: Darwin says it is not enough to show that species change; we must also explain how animals and plants fit their lives so well, as the woodpecker and the mistletoe do.

beats.scene: A pen underlines one careful sentence on a page of the manuscript
beats.summary: Darwin says he is convinced that natural selection has been the main means of change, but not the only one.

beats.scene: A hand points at a simple plan of chapters laid out on a table
beats.summary: Darwin outlines his plan: the tame and the wild, the struggle for life, natural selection, the difficulties of his theory, and then the evidence from rocks, geography and the body.

beats.scene: Two scales on a table, one heavy with facts, one with objections
beats.summary: Darwin admits that almost every point could be met by facts that seem to point the other way, and asks readers to weigh both sides fairly.

beats.scene: A green field of cows, sheep and horses at the start of a day
beats.summary: Darwin chooses to begin at home, with the farm animals and garden plants that people have kept for ages, because there change can be watched.

beats.scene: Wild plants and a tame garden side by side, with a gardener between them
beats.summary: Darwin explains that tame animals and plants vary far more than wild ones do, which makes them the best place to study change.

beats.scene: Many dogs of different sizes and shapes sit side by side on a lawn
beats.summary: Dogs range from tiny lapdogs to huge hounds; Darwin thought they came from several wild kinds, but later research shows they come from wolves.

beats.scene: Pigeons of many odd shapes sit together on the roof of a loft
beats.summary: Darwin keeps every kind of fancy pigeon he can find, including the fantail, the pouter, the carrier and the tumbler.

beats.scene: A bird expert looks in wonder at a row of very different pigeons
beats.summary: Darwin says that if the fancy pigeons were found wild, an expert would rank at least a dozen of them as separate species.

beats.scene: A grey wild pigeon on a sea cliff, with fancy breeds faintly behind
beats.summary: Many breeders think each breed had its own wild ancestor, but Darwin shows that would need eight or nine unknown wild species, and he argues that all came from the rock pigeon.

beats.scene: A blue-grey pigeon with two black wing bars beside two white fancy birds
beats.summary: The rock pigeon is slate blue with two black wing bars and a white back, and when Darwin crosses odd breeds, the young often show these same marks.

beats.scene: Darwin holds the skeleton of a pigeon next to the skeleton of another breed
beats.summary: Breeds differ in beak, skull, ribs, feet and the number of tail feathers, yet all can breed together freely, which suggests they belong to one species.

beats.scene: A red and green jungle fowl and a plump farmyard hen face each other
beats.summary: Darwin concludes that all the many kinds of farmyard chicken came from one wild bird of south-east Asia, the red jungle fowl.

beats.scene: A gardener holds up apples, plums and roses of many kinds
beats.summary: Garden plants such as apples, roses and cabbages also come in countless forms, each kept going by gardeners who choose the ones they like.

beats.scene: A shepherd looks at a lamb that is quite unlike its parents
beats.summary: Darwin admits that nobody understands why a young animal is like its parents or why it sometimes is not; the rules of inheritance are still mysterious.

beats.scene: A breeder in a barn looks closely at two animals before choosing one
beats.summary: Darwin explains that people do not create new variations; they pick the ones they like and breed from those, and so shape their animals.

beats.scene: A man in a sheep pen holds a prize ram while others admire it
beats.summary: A writer on farm animals, William Youatt, calls selection the magician's wand that lets a farmer change his flock altogether.

beats.scene: A little spaniel in old royal clothes sits beside a modern one
beats.summary: Even when people have no plan, keeping the best animals slowly changes them; the King Charles spaniel and the racehorse have both changed this way.

beats.scene: A famous breeder stands among his pigeons, counting years on his fingers
beats.summary: Good breeders see tiny differences that others miss; Sir John Sebright said he could breed any feather in three years but would need six for the head and beak.

beats.scene: A wall built brick by brick, with a breeder's hand adding the last brick
beats.summary: Nature supplies small changes, and people add them up in one direction, generation after generation, until the animal is very different from its ancestors.

beats.scene: A nurseryman checks a row of young seedlings, choosing one with bright flowers
beats.summary: A gardener cannot order a certain flower, but can pick the seedlings that please him, and sometimes sudden changes appear, as when a peach tree bears a nectarine.

beats.scene: Three very different sheep stand in a row under a wide sky
beats.summary: The results are striking: new breeds of sheep and cattle were made by selecting, and one writer said it looked as though breeders had chalked a perfect form on a wall and given it life.

beats.scene: A strange puffed-up pigeon struggles to fly against a strong wind
beats.summary: Breeders choose features that please them, not features that help the animal, so many fancy breeds might not survive well in the wild.

beats.scene: A farmer looks at cows grazing in new pasture under a changing sky
beats.summary: Darwin suggests that new conditions, such as different food, climate or care, make animals and plants vary more, but he admits he is not sure why.

beats.scene: A pigeon loft and a wild cliff face linked by a long winding road
beats.summary: If breeders can change animals this much in a few centuries, what could nature do over a very long time with every creature struggling to live?

beats.scene: Oak leaves on a table, each one a little different from the others
beats.summary: In the wild, too, no two creatures are exactly alike, and these small individual differences give natural selection something to work with.

beats.scene: Two scholars frown over a drawer of nearly identical butterflies
beats.summary: Naturalists cannot agree on what a species is, and experts looking at the same plants or animals often disagree over which are species and which only varieties.

beats.scene: A magnifying glass over two almost identical barnacles on a laboratory table
beats.summary: Darwin knows the problem first hand from his years with barnacles, where he often could not tell where one species ended and a variety began.

beats.scene: A ladder of leaves from a small difference to a large one
beats.summary: Darwin sees a ladder: slight individual differences lead to varieties, varieties to well-marked varieties, and these, he says, may lead to species.

beats.scene: A thick tree with many branches, some crowded and some almost bare
beats.summary: Darwin checks plant lists from several countries and finds that bigger groups of species have more varieties than smaller ones, which suggests that new species are forming there now.

beats.scene: A wide meadow of a common wildflower, with a few rare ones hidden below
beats.summary: Species that are common and spread over wide areas vary most, since they have more individuals and meet more conditions.

beats.scene: A cluster of similar small flowers growing around one larger plant
beats.summary: Close relatives in large groups tend to cluster tightly around one species, just as varieties cluster around the original form.

beats.scene: A hand writes the word species and then crosses it out lightly
beats.summary: Darwin says he sees the word species as a term used for convenience, for a group of creatures that closely resemble each other, and not as something fixed in nature.

beats.scene: A botanist and a naturalist compare long lists of plants by lamplight
beats.summary: His friend Hooker, a botanist, helps him with plant lists from many lands, and the same pattern turns up again and again.

beats.scene: A staircase of stone steps rising from a meadow to a hilltop
beats.summary: The ladder from individual differences to species is there for anyone to see, but what could keep the useful steps and let the rest go? The struggle for life is the answer.

beats.scene: A crowded hillside of tiny seedlings with fallen seeds and a few shoots
beats.summary: Chapter III begins with the struggle for existence: far more young are born than can survive, an idea Darwin takes from Malthus.

beats.scene: A plant drops two seeds on bare ground, with rows of plants behind it
beats.summary: Even a plant that makes only two seeds a year, said the naturalist Linnaeus, would have a million descendants in twenty years if all survived.

beats.scene: A mother elephant and her calf walk across open grassland at sunset
beats.summary: The slowest breeder known, the elephant, would still have about nineteen million descendants after about 750 years, if all of them survived.

beats.scene: Wild horses gallop across a wide plain in South America
beats.summary: Horses and cattle brought to South America ran wild and multiplied wonderfully fast, a sign of how quickly any kind can increase when conditions allow.

beats.scene: Small birds sing in a hedge while another eats a caterpillar
beats.summary: We forget that the birds singing around us mostly live by killing insects and seeds, so death is always at work behind nature's pleasant face.

beats.scene: Birds lie frozen in the snow on a wintry lawn at Down
beats.summary: The hard winter of 1854 to 1855 killed about four out of every five birds in Darwin's own grounds, which shows how sharply cold can reduce numbers.

beats.scene: Darwin kneels on a lawn marking tiny seedlings with little sticks
beats.summary: Darwin marks the weed seedlings that come up on a patch of cleared ground and finds that most are destroyed, mainly by slugs and insects.

beats.scene: A patch of mown turf with some plants strong and others fading
beats.summary: On a small plot of mown turf, Darwin finds that when the grass was left to grow freely, nine of the twenty kinds of plant died out, choked by the stronger ones.

beats.scene: A heath with fir seedlings inside a fence and bare ground outside it
beats.summary: Cattle can protect a heath from trees: where a fence keeps them out, thousands of young pines spring up; where they graze, there are none.

beats.scene: A dry plant at the edge of a desert with sand blowing around it
beats.summary: Darwin says he uses the struggle for existence in a large sense: a plant at a desert's edge may be said to struggle for life against the drought.

beats.scene: A cat, a mouse, a bumblebee and a clover flower joined by thin lines
beats.summary: Darwin shows how living things depend on each other in chains: cats eat mice, mice destroy bumblebee nests, bumblebees pollinate clover.

beats.scene: A fly lays eggs on a newborn calf while small birds hunt nearby
beats.summary: In Paraguay, a fly that lays its eggs in newborn animals prevents cattle and horses from living wild; the fly's own numbers depend on insect-eating birds and other creatures.

beats.scene: A surface studded with thousands of wedges, each hammered in by a heavy mallet
beats.summary: Darwin compares nature to a surface packed with ten thousand wedges, each driven in by blows, so that when one is knocked out another is driven in.

beats.scene: Two similar thrushes face each other on a hedge in rain
beats.summary: The fiercest struggle is between close relatives, since they need the same food and places; in Scotland the missel-thrush spread and the song-thrush grew fewer.

beats.scene: Sheep of two mountain varieties graze apart on a stony hillside
beats.summary: Even different varieties of one kind compete: some varieties of mountain sheep are said to starve out others, and mixed varieties of wheat can dwindle until only one is left.

beats.scene: A stingless native bee flies away from a swarm of honeybees in a tree
beats.summary: When people bring a new species to a new country, it can push out old inhabitants; Darwin says the hive bee is quickly exterminating a small native stingless bee in Australia.

beats.scene: A thinning flock of birds on a bare branch, with few left
beats.summary: When a kind of animal or plant becomes rare, it has taken the first step toward vanishing; Darwin says rarity is the forerunner of extinction.

beats.scene: Travellers on a mountain track see a plant growing thinner as they climb
beats.summary: When a species grows rarer toward the edge of its range, we blame the climate, but Darwin says rivals and enemies often matter more, since each species suffers heavy losses everywhere.

beats.scene: A calm meadow at dawn with birds, insects and flowers all alive
beats.summary: Darwin says we may take comfort: the war of nature is not constant, fear is not felt, death is usually quick, and the healthy and strong survive and multiply.

beats.scene: A scale tips slightly toward one of two almost identical seedlings
beats.summary: With so many born and so few surviving, even a tiny advantage may decide who lives, and Darwin asks whether this alone could shape living things.

beats.scene: A breeder's hand and a wild mountain landscape with a tiny hawk circling
beats.summary: Chapter IV asks a bold question: since useful variations for people have appeared, could useful variations for living creatures themselves not appear over many thousands of generations?

beats.scene: Two young animals race for food, one a little quicker than the other
beats.summary: Darwin names the process natural selection: favourable variations are kept and harmful ones are lost; Wallace later suggested the phrase survival of the fittest.

beats.scene: A grey wolf runs hard across a snowy plain after a deer
beats.summary: Darwin imagines a hard season when food is short: the swiftest and slimmest wolves would catch the most prey and be likelier to live and have pups.

beats.scene: Two wolves, one slim and light and one heavy, in a mountain forest
beats.summary: In the Catskill Mountains Darwin heard of two kinds of wolf, a light, greyhound-like one that chases deer and a heavier, shorter-legged one that attacks sheep.

beats.scene: A bee drinks nectar from a flower and carries yellow pollen on its legs
beats.summary: A flower that makes a sweet nectar attracts insects that carry its pollen; plants that make more nectar get more visits and leave more young.

beats.scene: A magnifying glass moves slowly over a hillside of plants and animals
beats.summary: Natural selection works every day and every hour, throughout the world, on even the slightest changes, rejecting the bad and keeping the good, silently and without being seen.

beats.scene: A fancy pigeon in a breeder's hand beside a wild bird in the wind
beats.summary: A breeder chooses only for his own good and looks only at the outside; nature chooses for the good of the creature itself, and for the whole body, and has far more time.

beats.scene: Two stags with great antlers fight in a misty valley while a doe watches
beats.summary: Darwin adds sexual selection: males compete for mates, as stags fight and as birds show off; the winners leave more young, so showy tails like the peacock's may have grown this way.

beats.scene: A pen rests on a page where the word selection is underlined
beats.summary: Darwin warns that natural selection is a figure of speech: nature means the laws of the world and selection means that some survive; it does not make changes, it only keeps the useful ones.

beats.scene: A clock hand turns slowly above a long row of old rolling hills
beats.summary: Natural selection works so slowly that we cannot watch it in action; we see the changes only when the hand of time has marked the long lapse of ages.

beats.scene: Two plots of grass, one with a single kind and one with many kinds
beats.summary: Darwin explains divergence: the more different descendants become from each other, the less they compete, so one place can feed more kinds; a plot with many kinds of grass yields more than a plot with one.

beats.scene: A meat-eating animal in a crowded land hunts in trees and water
beats.summary: Darwin imagines a flesh-eating animal in a crowded country: some of its descendants take to new prey, in trees or water, and slowly become different from the rest.

beats.scene: Darwin's single drawing: a spreading fan of branching lines over a row of letters
beats.summary: The only picture in the book is a diagram: a row of letters A to L at the base stands for species, and branching lines rise above it to show how some give rise to many new forms.

beats.scene: Branching lines rise through numbered levels, with some stopping and others spreading
beats.summary: In the diagram, each level stands for a thousand or more generations, and as the lines rise, most of them stop, while a few spread into whole families of new species.

beats.scene: A great tree with old bare branches, green buds and fallen twigs beneath
beats.summary: Darwin compares the whole history of life to a great tree: the green twigs are living species, and the earlier ones that died stand for extinct species; the branches were once twigs themselves.

beats.scene: A tree with old bare branches, green buds and fallen twigs below
beats.summary: As new forms spread, the older forms that they replace grow rare and die out, so natural selection and extinction go hand in hand.

beats.scene: A woodpecker walks on open grassland where almost no trees grow
beats.summary: Habits can change as well as bodies; Darwin saw a woodpecker on the treeless plains of La Plata that never climbs trees but is a woodpecker in every part of its body.

beats.scene: A bird with a wide cliff behind, with newcomers arriving from the sea
beats.summary: Selection makes a creature fit for its own home, not perfect; in New Zealand, native plants and animals have often lost to newcomers from Europe.

beats.scene: A broad grassy continent beside a small island that is separate from the land
beats.summary: New forms are most likely to arise in large areas with many individuals, but isolation, as on an island, helps a new form keep its features.

beats.scene: Three chain links labelled variation, inheritance and struggle hold up a seedling
beats.summary: Darwin sums it up: creatures vary, the useful variations are inherited, and since more are born than live, the best-fitted tend to survive; that is natural selection.

beats.scene: Darwin at his desk with a puzzled face and a crossed-out page
beats.summary: Chapter V opens with an honest admission: when Darwin speaks of chance variations, the word only shows that he does not know the cause of each one.

beats.scene: A wild duck flies over a pond beside a heavy farmyard duck
beats.summary: Use and disuse change the body: Darwin weighed the bones of wild and tame ducks and found that the tame duck's wing bones are lighter and its leg bones heavier.

beats.scene: A rabbit and a pig with floppy ears stand beside their wild relatives
beats.summary: Darwin suggests that the drooping ears of many tame animals come from disuse, because tame animals are seldom alarmed and so do not often prick up their ears.

beats.scene: A pale blind fish and a beetle crawl in the dark of a cave
beats.summary: Many cave animals, such as beetles and fish, have lost their sight, which Darwin explains mainly by disuse, since eyes are useless in the dark.

beats.scene: A white cat with blue eyes sleeps on a cushion in a sunny window
beats.summary: Parts of the body can change together; Darwin notes that white cats with blue eyes are often deaf, and that pigeons with short beaks tend to have small feet.

beats.scene: A peacock with spread feathers beside a plainer peahen
beats.summary: Showy features that set males apart, such as bright feathers, vary a great deal from one animal to the next, which gives selection plenty to work on.

beats.scene: A dun horse with a dark back stripe and faint bars on its legs
beats.summary: Dun-coloured horses of many breeds show a dark stripe down the back and bars on the legs, which Darwin takes as a return to a striped ancestor.

beats.scene: Two close relatives side by side, one with more variable marks than the other
beats.summary: Features that distinguish one species from its close cousins tend to vary more than features shared by the whole group.

beats.scene: A balance tipped with a long horn on one side and a short tail
beats.summary: Darwin suggests an economy of growth: if nature spends a great deal on one part, it must save on another, so a very large feature may mean a smaller one elsewhere.

beats.scene: Darwin closes a heavy notebook and looks out of the window at dusk
beats.summary: Darwin ends the chapter by admitting that our ignorance of the laws of variation is profound, and that in hardly one case in a hundred can we say why a part has varied.

beats.scene: Darwin sits alone with a long list of questions and a lit candle
beats.summary: Chapter VI is where Darwin turns critic of himself and lists the main difficulties of his theory before the reader can raise them.

beats.scene: A wide landscape where two big groups of animals meet at a narrow border
beats.summary: If species came from each other by small steps, why are there not countless in-between forms? Darwin answers that in-between varieties are few and are crowded out by the large groups on either side.

beats.scene: A large human eye next to a tiny light-sensing spot on a simple worm
beats.summary: Darwin admits that an organ as perfect as the eye seems, at first sight, absurdly unlikely to have been made by natural selection.

beats.scene: A row of eyes, from a flat light spot to a round lens
beats.summary: But Darwin points out that living animals show every step: from a simple nerve covered with colour, to eyes with lenses, and each step is useful to its owner.

beats.scene: A heavy sheet of paper with one bold sentence underlined twice
beats.summary: Darwin sets his own test: if any complex organ could be shown that could not possibly have been formed by many small steps, his theory would break down.

beats.scene: A flying squirrel glides between two trees with its skin stretched wide
beats.summary: Darwin imagines gliding by steps: squirrels with a slightly flattened tail, others with a fold of skin, and flying squirrels with a wide sheet between their legs.

beats.scene: A fish with a swim bladder beside a lung from an air-breathing animal
beats.summary: Parts can change their job: the swim bladder that helps a fish float can become a lung for breathing air, which shows how one organ may be turned to a new use.

beats.scene: A tall giraffe reaches high into a tree while shorter animals look up
beats.summary: Darwin imagines how a giraffe's long neck and legs might help it to reach high leaves in a time of drought, though scientists still discuss the details.

beats.scene: A small stepping stone path crossing a stream with no big jumps
beats.summary: Natural selection can act only by taking advantage of slight successive changes and can never take a leap, but must advance by the shortest and slowest steps.

beats.scene: A tired Darwin looks up from his pages at a field of stars
beats.summary: Darwin ends the chapter humbly: we are much too ignorant of how any creature lives to say which small changes would be useful, so the difficulties are real but not final.

beats.scene: A newborn chick pecks at seed straight after hatching, with no teacher near
beats.summary: Chapter VII turns to instincts: actions that animals perform without being taught and without knowing why, and that Darwin says vary and are inherited like parts of the body.

beats.scene: A young pointer dog freezes, nose out and paw lifted, at a field edge
beats.summary: Tame animals show how instincts can be shaped: a young pointer dog points at game the first time it is taken out, and tumbler pigeons somersault without being taught.

beats.scene: A tame bird lets a visitor come near while another flies away
beats.summary: Fear of man is an instinct that is learned slowly: on far islands like the Galapagos, where people had seldom lived, Darwin found that birds showed almost no fear of him.

beats.scene: A young cuckoo in a small nest pushes the other eggs over the edge
beats.summary: The cuckoo lays its egg in another bird's nest, and the newly hatched cuckoo pushes out the other eggs and chicks; Darwin suggests this instinct grew from small steps.

beats.scene: Red ants carry white pupae from a black ants' nest to their own
beats.summary: Darwin describes slave-making ants, which raid the nests of other ants, carry off the young, and raise them as workers; he watched this himself in southern England.

beats.scene: A honeycomb with rows of perfect six-sided cells filled with golden honey
beats.summary: The honeybee builds a comb of six-sided cells, which use the least wax and hold the most honey; Darwin calls the instinct one of the most wonderful known.

beats.scene: Three kinds of bees with three kinds of cells, from pots to hexagons
beats.summary: Darwin shows a ladder of bees: humble-bees use rough round pots, a tropical bee makes neat round cells in order, and the hive bee makes six-sided cells; the steps show how the instinct might have grown.

beats.scene: Soap-like bubbles pressed together make flat walls between six-sided cells
beats.summary: Darwin explains that if round cells are made at equal distances and overlap, the flat walls between them form six-sided shapes, so bees need only simple instincts to save wax.

beats.scene: A worker ant carries food past a large queen in a dark nest
beats.summary: Sterile worker ants and bees are Darwin's worst difficulty: they differ from their parents and cannot have young themselves, so how could selection improve them?

beats.scene: A farmer carves roast meat at a table while a bull stands outside
beats.summary: Darwin solves it by pointing to the family: just as a breeder keeps a stock whose meat was tasty even after the animal is gone, nature favours colonies whose workers are useful.

beats.scene: A horse and a donkey stand side by side with a mule between them
beats.summary: Chapter VIII asks why different species, when crossed, usually produce young that cannot have young themselves, while varieties of one species cross freely.

beats.scene: A strong mule pulls a cart along a country road
beats.summary: The mule, the young of a donkey and a horse, is strong and hardy but is nearly always sterile, which makes it the best-known example.

beats.scene: A row of flowers on a table with careful notes about crossing them
beats.summary: But sterility comes in all degrees; careful experimenters on plants, such as Kolreuter and Gartner, found everything from complete failure to full fertility.

beats.scene: Two pollen brushes are swapped between a tall and a short flower
beats.summary: A cross sometimes works in one direction but not the other: pollen of species A may fertilise species B easily, while pollen of B cannot fertilise A.

beats.scene: A big showy flower beside a small plain flower that cross with ease
beats.summary: How easily two species can be crossed does not depend on how different they look; very different species may cross, while very similar ones may not.

beats.scene: A balance weighing a hybrid animal that benefits nobody
beats.summary: Hybrid sterility cannot have been built up by natural selection, since it does no good to the individual; it must be a side effect of other differences.

beats.scene: Breeds of pigeons mate in a loft, though they look very different
beats.summary: All the breeds of pigeons, though they differ more than many wild species, breed together freely; the same is true of dogs, cattle and chickens.

beats.scene: Two apparently similar varieties meet in a field, but only a few seeds form
beats.summary: Darwin admits some exceptions: certain varieties of plants are partly infertile when crossed, so the line between varieties and species is not perfectly sharp.

beats.scene: A scientist of today looks at chromosomes through a microscope
beats.summary: Today biologists know that infertility between species arises from differences in genes and chromosomes, which Darwin did not know; modern science agrees that it is a by-product of change.

beats.scene: Darwin turns away from a chart of crosses, looking calm and satisfied
beats.summary: Darwin sums up: sterility is not a special gift but follows from differences in the reproductive system, so hybrids are not a threat to his theory.

beats.scene: Darwin faces a cliff of rock layers while holding a small hammer
beats.summary: Chapter IX asks why the rocks do not show the countless in-between forms that his theory expects; Darwin answers that the record of the rocks is very incomplete.

beats.scene: A ruined library with most books missing and torn pages on the floor
beats.summary: Darwin compares the record in the rocks to a history of the world kept badly, of which we have only the last volume, with a few chapters and a few lines on each page.

beats.scene: A geologist sits on a hill beside a thick book of geology
beats.summary: To understand the argument, Darwin says we must grasp the immense length of time; anyone who cannot feel it should read Lyell and then close his book.

beats.scene: A broad valley between two lines of chalk hills in southern England
beats.summary: Darwin tries to measure time by the slow wearing away of the Weald, a district in south-east England, and gets a figure of hundreds of millions of years, though he later withdrew it as uncertain.

beats.scene: Shells and bones sink into soft mud on a quiet sea floor
beats.summary: Fossils form only in special conditions: a creature must be buried quickly in mud or sand, usually under water, before it rots or is eaten.

beats.scene: A land animal lies on dry ground where scavengers have taken its bones
beats.summary: Land animals and soft-bodied creatures are especially rare as fossils, because they usually rot or are eaten and seldom end up in the mud of a lake or the sea.

beats.scene: Layers of rock lifted into a cliff, with gaps between layers marked by lines
beats.summary: Rock layers build up in patches over long periods and are then lifted, worn and lost, so that the record is full of gaps, some of which last longer than the layers themselves.

beats.scene: A small feathered fossil with teeth and a long bony tail in pale stone
beats.summary: Since Darwin wrote, finds like Archaeopteryx, a creature found in Germany in 1861 with feathers and teeth, have shown the kind of in-between form he expected.

beats.scene: Groups of animals appear in a layer of rock as if just arrived
beats.summary: Some groups seem to appear suddenly in the rocks, but Darwin says they might have arrived from places where earlier layers are missing or not yet found.

beats.scene: Darwin holds a few fossil shells and smiles gently at them
beats.summary: Darwin concludes that the gaps in the record are exactly what his theory predicts, and that, rather than damaging it, they are a reminder of how much of the past we have lost.

beats.scene: Rock layers with different fossils in each, old below and young above
beats.summary: Chapter X shows that fossils appear in order, older below and younger above; new species appear slowly one by one, and a kind that has died out never comes back.

beats.scene: A small group of animals stands on a shrinking patch of grass
beats.summary: Species do not usually vanish suddenly; they become rare first and then die out, so Darwin says we should not be astonished at extinction.

beats.scene: Darwin finds a horse's tooth in a cliff beside bones of giant animals
beats.summary: Darwin himself found a horse's tooth in South American rocks beside the bones of giant extinct animals, though horses had been gone from the continent until Europeans brought them back.

beats.scene: Fossil shells in layers, with older ones very different from living shells
beats.summary: The older the rocks, the more their fossils differ from living things; layers close together in time have fossils that resemble each other more than layers far apart.

beats.scene: A huge fossil shell of armour beside a small living armadillo
beats.summary: In South America the fossil animals, such as giant armadillo-like creatures, resemble the living animals of the same land; Darwin calls this the wonderful relationship between the dead and the living.

beats.scene: A cave in Australia with ancient bones of kangaroo-like animals
beats.summary: The same rule holds in Australia, where the fossil animals in caves are of the pouched kind, like the kangaroos that still live there.

beats.scene: A fossil with the features of two different animal groups, in pale stone
beats.summary: Fossils often fill the gaps between living groups, so the divisions among living animals look sharper than they once were.

beats.scene: A small shell of the lamp-shell kind, unchanged in old and new rocks
beats.summary: Some creatures, like the lamp-shell Lingula, have changed very little since the oldest rocks, which shows that species change at very different speeds.

beats.scene: A bare rock layer with a first crowd of complex fossils and nothing below
beats.summary: Darwin admits a real puzzle: whole groups of animals seem to appear suddenly in the oldest fossil-bearing rocks, with no earlier ancestors, though simpler fossils have since been found in older rocks.

beats.scene: Darwin looks at a long chart of fossils arranged from old to young
beats.summary: Darwin says the imperfect record still agrees with his idea: fossils follow the pattern of a family tree, and the history of life is a story of descent.

beats.scene: A map of the world with two lands of similar climate but different animals
beats.summary: Chapters XI and XII ask why places with the same climate can hold different creatures; Darwin says a likeness of climate does not explain the living things of a region.

beats.scene: A narrow land bridge with different fish in the seas on either side
beats.summary: Barriers such as seas, deserts and mountains mark the edges of regions, and creatures on either side differ; the fish on the two sides of Panama are mostly different.

beats.scene: A single tree in a clearing, with seeds blowing out across the land
beats.summary: Darwin supposes that each species began in one place and spread outward as far as barriers and rivals allowed, so creatures must have ways to travel.

beats.scene: Seeds float in a bowl of salt water on a garden table
beats.summary: Darwin soaks the seeds of dozens of plants in salt water for weeks, and finds that many sprout afterwards, so seeds could cross a sea on currents.

beats.scene: A bird stands in a pond while mud sticks to its feet
beats.summary: Darwin finds that mud on birds' feet can carry seeds too: a few spoonfuls of pond mud grew a surprising number of plants, so birds may carry plants between ponds and islands.

beats.scene: Ice and snow cover a plain while cold-loving plants grow low among the stones
beats.summary: During the Ice Age, cold-climate plants and animals spread south; when the weather warmed, they climbed mountains or moved north, which is why the same kinds live on distant mountain tops and in the Arctic.

beats.scene: A lonely ocean island with birds and insects but no frogs or deer
beats.summary: Remote oceanic islands have few kinds of living things: no frogs, toads or newts, and no land mammals except bats, which can fly there, whereas creatures that cannot cross salt water are missing.

beats.scene: Two groups of volcanic islands, one near America and one near Africa
beats.summary: The Galapagos creatures resemble those of South America and the Cape Verde Islands creatures resemble those of Africa, though the two island groups have very similar climates and rocks.

beats.scene: A finch and a mockingbird are different on each of three islands
beats.summary: Within the Galapagos, each island has its own kinds of mockingbird and finch, which are close relatives, and many live nowhere else on Earth.

beats.scene: A beetle with no wings crawls in the wind on a rocky Atlantic island
beats.summary: On windy islands like Madeira, many beetles have lost their wings, which Darwin explains because flying insects were blown out to sea and wingless ones survived.

beats.scene: A large chart with groups of animals inside bigger groups, like nested circles
beats.summary: Chapter XIII starts with classification: naturalists sort living things into groups within groups, and Darwin says the hidden bond that makes this possible is descent from common ancestors.

beats.scene: A whale swims through blue water beside a fish and a dolphin
beats.summary: Classification looks at deep likeness and not outward looks: a whale looks like a fish, but naturalists place it with the mammals, because it feeds its young with milk.

beats.scene: A tiny swimming larva beside an adult barnacle fixed to a rock
beats.summary: Darwin's own work on barnacles shows the point: grown barnacles look like shellfish, but their young swim like little crustaceans, which reveals what they are.

beats.scene: A human hand, a bat's wing, a horse's leg and a porpoise's flipper
beats.summary: A human hand, a bat's wing, a horse's leg and a porpoise's flipper are all built from the same set of bones, which is easy to understand if all share one ancestor.

beats.scene: A beetle, a bee and a butterfly with their mouth parts drawn beside them
beats.summary: The same pattern appears elsewhere: the jaws of a beetle and the long tongue of a butterfly are made from the same parts, and the parts of a flower are altered leaves.

beats.scene: Tiny embryos of a fish, a bird and a mammal lie side by side
beats.summary: Young embryos of animals with backbones look very much alike; the great embryologist von Baer said he could not tell which class his unlabelled embryos belonged to.

beats.scene: A diagram links the growing stages of an animal to its ancestors
beats.summary: Darwin suggests that an embryo is a kind of picture, more or less hidden, of the ancestor of its group, which explains why young animals of related kinds look alike.

beats.scene: A calf's mouth showing small teeth that never cut through the gum
beats.summary: Many animals carry small useless parts called rudimentary organs: unborn calves have teeth that never cut through the gum, and some birds have tiny useless wings.

beats.scene: A page of old handwriting with silent letters in pale ink
beats.summary: Darwin compares a rudimentary organ to a letter in a word that is still written but no longer sounded; it is useless now but offers a clue to where the word came from.

beats.scene: A tangle of paths joining a hand, a wing, an embryo and a tooth
beats.summary: Darwin sums up: descent with modification explains classification, matching limbs, similar embryos and leftover organs all at once, which is the mark of a good theory.

beats.scene: Darwin looks over a table full of his pages, charts and notes
beats.summary: In Chapter XIV, Darwin gathers the whole book together; he calls it one long argument from beginning to end.

beats.scene: A single lamp lights many scattered pages that all point one way
beats.summary: Darwin argues that one idea, descent with modification through natural selection, explains many separate facts at once, which is what makes a good theory.

beats.scene: A crowd of older scholars in dark coats shakes their heads at a youth
beats.summary: Darwin expects older naturalists, whose minds are full of facts seen the old way, to disagree, and he puts his hope in younger ones who can look at both sides.

beats.scene: A single bright sentence glows on a page with a distant crowd behind
beats.summary: In one short sentence, Darwin says that light will be thrown on the origin of man and his history, but he says nothing more about humans in this book.

beats.scene: A wild bank thickly covered with plants, birds, insects and worms in morning light
beats.summary: Darwin pictures a tangled bank covered with many kinds of plants, with birds singing in the bushes, insects flitting about and worms crawling through the damp earth.

beats.scene: A sunlit hillside spread out below a great tree of branching life
beats.summary: Darwin finds grandeur in this view of life, which began with a few simple forms and from a beginning so simple has grown endless forms most beautiful and wonderful.

beats.scene: Crowds in a London bookshop buy copies of a new green-bound book
beats.summary: The first printing of about 1,250 copies was bought up by booksellers almost at once, and a second edition of about 3,000 followed in January 1860.

beats.scene: Two men in black coats argue on a platform in an Oxford hall
beats.summary: Thomas Huxley defends the book as its chief champion; in June 1860 he and Bishop Wilberforce argued about it at Oxford, though accounts of what was said differ.

beats.scene: An old Darwin in a garden chair with a book on his knee
beats.summary: Darwin revises the book through six editions and writes many more, then dies on 19 April 1882, and is buried in Westminster Abbey near Isaac Newton.

beats.scene: A modern reader opens a worn copy of the book beneath a tree
beats.summary: The book changed science: later discoveries, such as genes and DNA, have corrected and enriched its ideas, but the core of its argument remains the foundation of modern biology.
