B1B2: Charles Darwin was born in Shrewsbury, England, on 12 February 1809. As a boy he was always collecting things, such as beetles, shells and stones, and he loved to walk in the countryside.

Darwin first studied medicine in Edinburgh, but he disliked it, so his father sent him to Cambridge to become a clergyman. There he spent his days collecting beetles and walking with a botany teacher called John Stevens Henslow.

In 1831 Captain Robert FitzRoy needed a companion and a naturalist for his ship, the Beagle, and Henslow suggested Darwin. His father said no at first, but Darwin's uncle, Josiah Wedgwood, helped to change his mind.
The Beagle sailed from Plymouth on 27 December 1831, with the young Darwin on board. The trip was planned to last two years, but it took nearly five, and Darwin was often badly seasick.

In Brazil, Darwin stepped into a tropical rainforest for the first time. He was amazed by the huge trees, the brilliant flowers and the endless number of insects, birds and plants all crowded together.

On the coast of South America, Darwin found enormous bones buried in the cliffs. They belonged to giant animals that no longer lived, yet they looked strangely like small armadillos and sloths that were still alive there.

In February 1835, while Darwin was resting in a forest in Chile, a strong earthquake shook the ground. Afterwards he saw that parts of the coast had been lifted up, leaving beds of dead shellfish above the high-tide line.

Crossing the Andes mountains, Darwin found fossil sea shells far above the level of the ocean. This agreed with a book by Charles Lyell, which taught that the land had changed slowly over a very long time.

In September 1835 the Beagle reached the Galapagos Islands, a group of volcanic islands far out in the Pacific Ocean. Darwin spent about five weeks there, collecting birds, plants, lizards and giant tortoises.

On the way home, Darwin studied the coral islands of the Indian Ocean and worked out how they were made. The Beagle reached Falmouth in England on 2 October 1836, and Darwin came ashore with thousands of specimens and many notebooks.

Back in London, Darwin gave his birds to an expert named John Gould. Gould told him that the Galapagos birds, which Darwin had thought were quite different, were a group of finches of about a dozen kinds.
In 1837 Darwin began a private notebook about how one kind of animal might slowly turn into another. On one page he drew a small branching tree, with the words I think written above it.

In 1838 Darwin read an essay by Thomas Malthus, who argued that human numbers grow faster than the food supply. Darwin suddenly saw that the same struggle must happen among all plants and animals, and that the survivors would pass on their useful qualities.
Darwin married his cousin Emma Wedgwood in January 1839, and they went on to have ten children. In 1842 the family moved to Down House, a quiet home in the countryside of Kent.

Behind Down House, Darwin had a gravel path called the Sandwalk, where he walked every day and let his thoughts wander. He was often ill, with stomach pains and great tiredness, so he could only work for a few hours at a time.

From about 1846, Darwin spent eight years studying barnacles, those small creatures that cling to rocks and ships. The work was long and tiring, but it showed him how much even close relatives can differ, and it made him a respected expert.
In 1844 Darwin wrote a long essay on his theory and asked Emma to have it published if he died. He told only a few friends, and he said to Joseph Hooker that it felt like confessing a murder.

Darwin began to keep fancy pigeons at Down, and he joined clubs of pigeon breeders to learn their secrets. He also wrote hundreds of letters to farmers, gardeners and travellers, asking them for facts about how plants and animals change.

In 1856 Charles Lyell warned Darwin that someone else might reach the same idea first, and he urged him to write it down. Darwin agreed, and he began a very large book on the subject called Natural Selection.

In 1857 Darwin wrote a long letter to Asa Gray, a botanist in America, and explained his idea to him in detail. Even then he still did not publish, because he wanted every part of his argument to be strong.

Alfred Russel Wallace was a British naturalist who earned his living by collecting insects, birds and animals for museums. From 1854 he spent about eight years travelling among the islands of south-east Asia.

In early 1858, while he lay ill with fever on the island of Ternate, Wallace remembered the book by Malthus. He saw at once that the strongest and best-suited animals would survive, and he wrote out his idea in a few evenings.

Wallace's essay reached Darwin at his home in Kent on 18 June 1858, after a long journey by sea. Darwin read it with growing alarm, because it described almost exactly the theory that he had been developing for twenty years.
Just ten days later, scarlet fever took the life of Darwin and Emma's baby son, Charles Waring. In his grief, Darwin could hardly think about the question of who should publish first.
Lyell and Hooker decided on a fair plan that would help both men. They would present Wallace's essay together with earlier writings by Darwin, so that both men would share the credit.
On 1 July 1858 the papers by Wallace and Darwin were read together at a meeting of the Linnean Society in London. Neither man was present, since Wallace was far away and Darwin stayed at home.

The reaction was very quiet indeed, and few listeners realised what they had just heard. At the end of the year, the Society's president said that the year had brought no striking discoveries, so little did people understand.
When Wallace heard what had happened, he was pleased and not angry at all. He admired Darwin's vast collection of facts, and many years later he even named one of his own books Darwinism.
Darwin put aside his huge unfinished book and began a shorter one, which he called an abstract. The work took about thirteen months, and it grew much longer than he had planned.

The publisher John Murray agreed to print the book, even before he had read it all. It came out on 24 November 1859 with a very long title that began On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection.
Darwin opens his Introduction by remembering the voyage of the Beagle. He says that facts he saw there made him ask about the origin of species, a question once called the mystery of mysteries.

Two groups of facts from the voyage stayed in Darwin's mind. One was how fossil animals resembled living ones of the same country, and the other was how island creatures differed from island to island.
Darwin tells the reader that he has thought about the subject for many years. This book is only a short summary, and he cannot give all his facts or sources, so he asks for trust.

In the Introduction, Darwin generously mentions Alfred Russel Wallace, who was then studying the animals and plants of south-east Asia. He says that Wallace had reached almost the same conclusions as himself.

In Darwin's day, most naturalists believed that every species was made separately and could never change. A few thinkers, including Erasmus Darwin and the French naturalist Lamarck, had suggested otherwise but could not explain how.
Darwin says it is not enough to show that species change. He also wants to explain how creatures fit their lives so well, like a woodpecker that finds insects and a mistletoe spread by birds.
Darwin states his conclusion clearly and with great care. He is convinced that natural selection has been the main means of change, but he does not say it is the only one.
Darwin now explains how the rest of his book will go. He will start with tame animals and plants, then turn to wild ones, the struggle for life, natural selection and the evidence.

Darwin admits that for almost every point he makes, someone could bring up facts that seem to prove the opposite. A fair judgement, he says, can come only from putting the facts and arguments on both sides of each question.

Having laid out his plan, Darwin begins in the most familiar place of all, the farm and the garden. Tame animals and plants have been kept by people for thousands of years, so they show change in a way that we can easily see.
Darwin points out that tame animals and plants differ from one another far more than wild ones do. That is why they are the best place to start looking for change.

Dogs range from tiny lapdogs to huge hounds, and from long-legged racers to short-legged diggers. Darwin thought they came from several wild kinds, although later research shows that they descend from wolves.

Darwin kept every breed of fancy pigeon that he could get, and he studied them closely. The fantail spreads a tail like a fan, the pouter puffs out its chest, and the tumbler turns somersaults in the air.
Darwin says that a bird expert could pick at least a dozen breeds that look completely different. If told they were wild birds, he would certainly call them separate species.
Some breeders believed each breed had its own wild ancestor, but Darwin found this unlikely. It would need eight or nine different wild pigeons, and nobody has ever found them.
The wild rock pigeon is slate blue, with two black bars on each wing. When Darwin crossed odd-coloured breeds, the young birds sometimes appeared in this very same blue colour, bars and all.

The breeds of pigeon differ in their beaks, skulls, ribs, feet and tails, and Darwin compared their skeletons. Even so, they can all breed together without any trouble, which suggests that they are one species.
Darwin did the same with chickens, which come in many shapes, sizes and colours. He concluded that all of them came from a single wild bird in south-east Asia, the red jungle fowl.
Garden plants show the same story, for apples, roses and cabbages all exist in countless forms. Gardeners have noticed new forms again and again, and they have kept the ones they liked best.
Darwin admits that the laws of inheritance are not well understood. Like usually produces like, but not always, and no one yet knew why a lamb should differ from its parents.
The secret of the breeder, Darwin says, is choice. People do not create new differences, but they pick the animals they like and breed only from those.
A writer on farm animals named William Youatt called selection the magician's wand. With it, he said, a farmer could change his whole flock into something quite different.
Often people change animals without meaning to, simply by keeping the best ones. The King Charles spaniel has changed a great deal since the days of that king, and so has the racehorse.
Expert breeders can see small differences that most of us would never notice. Sir John Sebright said he could breed any chosen feather in three years, but a new head and beak would take six.
Nature supplies the small changes, and people add them up in one direction. Over many generations, tiny steps can build an animal that looks quite different from its ancestors.
A gardener cannot order a new flower into being, but he can pick the best seedlings out of thousands. Sometimes a sudden change appears, as when a branch of a peach tree bears a nectarine.
Breeders have improved sheep and cattle in this way within a few generations. One writer said it seemed as if they had chalked a perfect shape on a wall and then given it life.
Breeders choose what pleases them, such as a fancy tail or a huge chest, and not what helps the animal live. Left to themselves in the wild, many of these birds might do badly.
Darwin thinks that new conditions, such as different food, climate or care, make animals and plants vary more. He admits, however, that he cannot say for certain why this should happen.
If breeders can change animals so much in a few hundred years, what might nature do in a far longer time? Darwin leaves the question hanging and turns from the farm to the wild.
Wild plants and animals vary just as tame ones do. No two leaves on a tree are exactly the same, and these small differences are the raw material for natural selection.
Naturalists have never agreed on a clear definition of a species. Two experts looking at the same plants may call one form a separate species while the other calls it a mere variety.
Darwin knew this puzzle at first hand from his years of work on barnacles. Again and again, he could not tell whether two forms were different species or only varieties of one.
Darwin sees a kind of ladder in the facts. Small individual differences lead to slight varieties, and slight varieties lead to well-marked ones, which may in time become new species.
Darwin studied lists of plants from several countries and found a clear pattern. The larger a group of related species is, the more varieties its members tend to have.
Darwin found that common species, living over wide areas, vary more than rare ones. This is not surprising, since they have more individuals and meet more kinds of conditions.
Darwin noticed that the species in large groups tend to cluster tightly around a few others. They are related to each other much as varieties are related to the form they came from.
Darwin says that he treats the term species as a handy label, given to a group of creatures that look very much alike. It does not, he thinks, describe something that is fixed forever in nature.
Darwin's friend Joseph Hooker, the botanist, helped him by supplying the plant lists of many lands. Whichever country they tried, the same pattern turned up again and again.
The ladder from small differences to species is there for anyone to see, and the next question is what could keep the useful steps. Darwin thinks the answer is the struggle for life.
Chapter III opens with the struggle for existence, an idea that Darwin borrows from Malthus. He applies it to all plants and animals: far more young are born than can ever survive.
The great naturalist Linnaeus worked out a simple sum for a plant that makes only two seeds a year. If every seed grew, he said, there would be a million plants after twenty years.
Darwin chose the elephant, one of the slowest breeders of all. If every elephant lived and had young, he calculated, one pair would have about nineteen million descendants after roughly 750 years.
Darwin had seen for himself how fast animals can multiply. Horses and cattle brought to South America ran wild and spread across the plains in huge numbers.
We see the face of nature as bright and cheerful, but we forget something. Most of the birds that sing so sweetly around us live by eating insects and seeds, so they are constantly destroying life.
Darwin saw for himself how cruel the weather can be. The hard winter of 1854 and 1855 killed about four out of every five birds in his own grounds, which was a terrible loss.
Darwin cleared a small patch of ground and marked every weed seedling that came up. Most of them were destroyed, chiefly by slugs and insects, and only a few survived.
Darwin watched a small plot of turf that had been mown short. When he let the grass grow freely, nine of the twenty kinds of plant died out, because the stronger ones crowded them.
Darwin describes a wide sandy heath where cattle fed on the plants. When a fence was built to keep the cattle out, thousands of young pine trees sprang up inside it, while outside there were none.
Darwin explains that he uses the word struggle in a wide sense. A plant growing at the edge of a desert may be said to struggle for life against the drought.
Darwin shows how living things depend on each other in long chains. Cats eat mice, mice destroy bumblebee nests, and bumblebees are the main visitors that can pollinate red clover.

In Paraguay, Darwin writes, a kind of fly lays its eggs on newborn cattle and horses, and so these animals cannot run wild there. The number of flies, in turn, depends on insect-eating birds and other creatures.
Darwin compares nature to a surface packed tight with ten thousand sharp wedges, driven in by endless blows. When one wedge is knocked out, another is hammered into the gap.

Darwin says the fiercest struggle is between close relatives, because they need the same food and the same places to live. In Scotland, he notes, as one kind of thrush increased, another kind became rarer.
Even varieties of the same kind may compete with one another. Some varieties of mountain sheep are said to starve out others, so that they cannot be kept together.
Newcomers brought in by people can upset the balance of nature too, Darwin says. The honeybee, taken to Australia, was said to be rapidly killing off a small native bee that has no sting.
Darwin points out that rarity comes before extinction in nature. When a species has become rare, a single bad season or a new enemy may be enough to finish it.

When we see a species grow rarer toward the edge of its range, we blame the climate. Darwin says that rivals and enemies are often just as important, because every species loses many members everywhere.
Darwin now offers the reader a gentler thought about all this struggle. The war of nature is not endless, he says, and death is usually quick, while the healthy and the happy survive.
With so many born and so few surviving, even a tiny advantage may decide who lives. Darwin ends the chapter by asking whether this alone could slowly change living things.

Chapter IV begins with a bold and simple question about nature. If changes useful to people have often appeared in tame animals, why should changes useful to the creatures themselves not appear in the wild?
Darwin now gives this process a proper name of its own. The keeping of helpful differences he calls natural selection, and later he also used the phrase survival of the fittest.
Darwin imagines a wolf in a hard season, when food is scarce. The swiftest and slimmest wolves would catch the most prey, so they would be likelier to survive and raise young.
Darwin heard that two kinds of wolf lived in the Catskill Mountains of America. One was light and greyhound-like and chased deer, while the other was bulkier, with shorter legs, and attacked sheep.
Darwin thinks of a flower that makes a sweet juice called nectar. Insects visiting it carry pollen to other flowers, and the plants with the most nectar get the most visits and the most seeds.
Darwin says that natural selection is watching every hour of every day, all over the world. It keeps what is good and rejects what is bad, working silently and unseen.
A breeder chooses only for his own benefit, and he sees only the outside of an animal. Nature chooses for the good of the creature itself, and she can act upon every part of it.
Darwin adds a second kind of choosing, which he calls sexual selection. Males that fight well, or that look most attractive to females, leave more young, and this may explain the peacock's tail.
Darwin warns that the words are only a figure of speech. Nature does not think or plan, and selection does not create changes, but only keeps the helpful ones that happen to appear.
These changes are so slow that no one can watch them happen. We see the result only when time has passed, like looking at the hour hand of a clock that has moved.

Darwin explains why living things tend to become more different from each other. The more they differ, the less they compete, so a plot sown with many kinds of grass feeds more plants than a plot with one.

Darwin imagines a meat-eating animal in a country that is already crowded. Some of its descendants would turn to new food, in trees or in water, and over time they would grow different from the others.
The only picture in Darwin's book is a diagram of branching lines. Letters from A to L stand for species of one group, and the lines show how some of them give rise to new forms.
In the diagram, the space between two levels stands for a thousand or more generations. As the lines rise, most of them stop short, but a few spread into new kinds.
Darwin compares the family tree of life to a great tree. The green buds are species alive today, and the dead twigs of former years stand for species that no longer exist.
As improved forms spread, they take the place of the older forms that they resemble most. In this way natural selection and extinction go hand in hand.
Darwin saw a woodpecker on the treeless plains of La Plata that hunts for food on the ground. In every part of its body it is a true woodpecker, but it never climbs a tree.
Natural selection makes each creature fit for its own home, but it does not make it perfect. In New Zealand, many native plants and animals have lost out to newcomers from Europe.
Darwin suggests that large lands, with many individuals, give more chances for useful changes to appear. Isolation, as on an island, helps a new form to keep its features without mixing back.

Darwin sums up his whole argument in three simple steps. Creatures vary, more are born than can live, and so those with useful differences will survive and pass those differences on, which is natural selection.
Chapter V begins with an honest admission by the author. Darwin has sometimes spoken as if variations were due to chance, but this only shows that he does not know their causes.
Darwin weighed the bones of wild and tame ducks. In the tame duck, which walks more and flies less, the wing bones were lighter and the leg bones heavier.

Many tame animals, such as rabbits, have ears that droop, while wild ones almost never do. Darwin thought the cause might be disuse, because tame animals are seldom alarmed and rarely raise their ears.
Many animals that live in dark caves, including beetles and fish, have lost their sight. Darwin thought that disuse was the main cause, since eyes are of little use in total darkness.
Parts of the body often change together, in ways that are hard to explain. Darwin notes that white cats with blue eyes are usually deaf, and that pigeons with short beaks tend to have small feet.
Darwin found that bright and showy features, which often set males apart from females, vary a great deal from one animal to the next. This gives selection plenty of material to work on.
Dun-coloured horses of many breeds sometimes have a dark stripe down the back and faint bars on the legs. Darwin took these marks as a sign that the ancestors of horses were striped.
Darwin notices that the features which tell close relatives apart vary more than the ones they all share. This is what we would expect if the species had only recently become different.
Darwin suggests that growth has a kind of economy. If nature spends a great deal on one part of the body, it may have to save on another.
Darwin ends the chapter with one more honest confession about his knowledge. Our ignorance of the laws of variation is profound, he says, and rarely can we say why a part has varied.
In Chapter VI, Darwin turns critic of his own theory. He lists the main difficulties himself, before any reader has the chance to raise them.
Why do we not see countless in-between forms, if species arose by small steps? Darwin replies that such varieties live on narrow borders and are crowded out by the large groups on either side.
Darwin openly admits that the human eye, with its many perfect parts, seems absurd to explain by natural selection. He says he feels the difficulty as strongly as anyone.
Yet Darwin points out that animals alive today show every step between a simple light-sensing nerve and a fine eye with a lens. Each step is useful to the animal that has it.
Darwin now sets a hard test for his own theory. If anyone could show a complex organ that could not have been formed by many small steps, he says, his theory would break down.
Darwin looks at flying squirrels, which glide from tree to tree on a wide fold of skin. He notes that other squirrels have flattened tails or small skin folds, and each step helps in leaping.
Darwin points out that parts can change their jobs. The swim bladder, which helps a fish to float, is related to the lungs that other animals use for breathing air.
Darwin thought that the giraffe's long neck and legs might have helped it to reach the high branches of trees in a time of drought. Scientists still discuss the details of how this happened.
Darwin states a rule that he says is true of natural selection: it can never take a leap. It must move forward by the shortest and slowest steps.
Darwin closes the chapter on a modest and careful note. We are too ignorant of how any creature lives, he says, to be sure which small changes would be useful or harmful.
Chapter VII is about instincts, the things that animals do without being taught. Darwin argues that instincts are inherited and can vary, just like parts of the body.
Tame animals show how instincts can be shaped by selection. A young pointer dog will point at game the very first time it is taken out, and young tumbler pigeons tumble without being taught.
Fear of man is an instinct that takes generations to form. On remote islands where people had seldom lived, such as the Galapagos, Darwin found that the birds were almost unafraid of him.
The cuckoo lays its eggs in other birds' nests, and the baby cuckoo, soon after hatching, pushes the other eggs and chicks out. Darwin thinks this instinct grew by many small steps.
Some ants are slave makers, Darwin tells his readers. They raid other ants' nests and carry off the young, and the stolen ants work in the raiders' nest, as Darwin saw in England.
The honeybee builds its comb from cells with six sides, which use the least wax and hold the most honey. Darwin calls this one of the most wonderful of all instincts.
Darwin shows a ladder of bees, from simple builders to expert ones. The humble-bee uses rough round pots, another bee builds neat round cells, and the hive bee makes six-sided ones.
Darwin explains that round cells, built close together at equal distances, will meet along flat walls. A few simple instincts are enough to produce the six-sided comb, and wax is saved.
Darwin calls the sterile worker ants and bees his worst difficulty. They differ greatly from their parents and never have young, so how could natural selection have shaped them?
Darwin solves the puzzle by looking at the whole family. A breeder can keep a stock whose meat was good, even after the animal is eaten, and nature can favour families whose workers are useful.

Chapter VIII faces a real puzzle about the fertility of crosses. Different species that are crossed usually have sterile young, but varieties of one species mate freely, so some thought this proved that species are separate.
The mule is the best-known hybrid, a cross between a horse and a donkey. It is strong and hardy and works well, but it is almost always unable to have young.

Careful experimenters who crossed plants, such as Kolreuter and Gartner, found that sterility comes in all degrees. Some crosses failed completely, some gave a few weak seeds, and some were nearly fertile.
Odd things happen in these experiments with crossing plants. Pollen of one species may easily fertilise a second species, while the pollen of the second cannot fertilise the first at all.
Darwin finds that how easily two species cross has little to do with how much they look alike. Some very different species can cross, while some very similar ones cannot.
Darwin argues that natural selection could not have created sterility, because it gives no advantage to an individual. It must be a side effect of other differences between species.
Even the strangest pigeon breeds can breed together without any trouble. The same is true of dogs, cattle and chickens, although many breeds differ more than some wild species.
Darwin admits that there are some exceptions to the rule. A few varieties of plants are partly infertile with each other, so the line between varieties and species is not perfectly sharp.

Today biologists know that infertility between species arises from differences in genes and chromosomes, which Darwin could not know. Their findings agree with his view that it is a by-product of change.
Darwin sums up the whole chapter with real confidence. Sterility is not a special gift that keeps species apart, he says, and so hybrids are no threat to his theory.
Chapter IX takes up another difficulty for the theory. If it is right, the rocks should hold countless in-between forms, but Darwin says the record of the rocks is very incomplete.
Darwin compares the rocks to a history book of the world that is badly kept. We have only the last volume, he says, and only a few chapters and a few lines on each page.
To follow his argument, Darwin says, we must grasp how immensely long the Earth's history has been. Anyone who cannot do so should read Lyell's book and then put down his own.
To give a sense of time, Darwin tried to work out how long it took rain and sea to wear away the Weald. He got hundreds of millions of years, but later withdrew the figure as uncertain.
Fossils form only in very special and rather rare conditions. A dead creature must be buried quickly in mud or sand, usually under water, before it rots or is eaten.
Land animals and soft-bodied creatures are especially rare as fossils. They usually rot or are eaten, and they seldom end up buried in the mud of a lake or sea.
Layers of rock pile up in patches over long periods, and then they are lifted, worn away and lost. The record is therefore full of gaps, some of them longer than the layers themselves.
Soon after the book appeared, a fossil called Archaeopteryx was found in Germany in 1861. It had feathers like a bird but also teeth and a long bony tail, like a reptile.
Some groups of animals seem to appear suddenly in one layer of rock. Darwin says they might have lived somewhere else for a long time before coming to the place where we find them.
Darwin concludes that the gaps in the record are just what his theory leads us to expect. They are not a proof against it, he says, but a reminder of how much of the past we have lost.
Chapter X looks at how fossils are arranged in time. New species appear slowly, one by one, and once a species has died out, Darwin says, it never comes back again.
Darwin says that species do not usually vanish suddenly. They become rare first, and then they die out one after another as new rivals spread.
In South America, Darwin himself found a horse's tooth in the rocks, lying beside the bones of giant extinct animals. Horses had vanished from the continent long before Europeans brought new ones.
Darwin found that the older the rocks, the more their fossils differ from living creatures. Layers that are close together in age contain fossils that resemble each other most.

In South America, the fossil animals look like larger cousins of the animals that live there today, such as armadillos and sloths. Darwin calls this the wonderful relationship between the dead and the living.
The same rule holds true in Australia, Darwin says. The fossil animals found in caves there are of the pouched kind, just like the kangaroos and their relatives that live there today.
Darwin points out that fossils often fill the gaps between groups of animals that are alive today. This makes the divisions between groups look less sharp than they would otherwise seem.
Some creatures, such as a small shellfish called Lingula, have changed very little since the oldest rocks. Species change at very different speeds, and some hardly change at all.
Darwin admits a real puzzle about the oldest fossils. The oldest fossil rocks already hold complex animals, with no ancestors below them, and he can give no answer yet.
Darwin concludes that even the imperfect fossil record fits his idea well. The fossils follow the pattern of a family tree, and the history of life is a story of descent.
Chapters XI and XII ask where living things live, and why. Two countries with the same climate can have quite different animals and plants, so climate alone cannot be the whole answer.
Great barriers such as seas, deserts and mountains mark the edges of regions, and creatures on either side differ. The sea animals on the two sides of Panama, for example, are mostly different.
Darwin supposes that each species began in just one place and then spread outward as far as it could. If this is true, living things must have many ways of travelling.
Darwin soaked the seeds of dozens of plants in salt water for weeks. Many of them still sprouted afterwards, so seeds could cross a sea on floating wood or on the sea itself.
Darwin also found that mud on birds' feet can carry seeds. A few spoonfuls of pond mud grew a surprising number of plants, so birds may carry plants from place to place.
During the great Ice Age, cold-loving plants and animals spread far to the south. When it warmed again, they climbed up mountains, so the same kinds now live on far-apart peaks and in the Arctic.
Far-off oceanic islands have few kinds of living things. They have no frogs, toads or newts and no land mammals, except bats, which can fly across the sea.
The Galapagos Islands and the Cape Verde Islands are both volcanic and warm. Yet Galapagos creatures resemble those of South America, while the Cape Verde creatures resemble those of Africa.
Within the Galapagos, each island has its own kinds of birds, which are close relatives of one another. Many of them live nowhere else on Earth, and Darwin saw this.
On windy islands such as Madeira, many beetles have lost their wings. Darwin explains this with natural selection, because those that flew were blown out to sea and those that did not survived.
Chapter XIII begins with the way scientists classify things. They sort living things into groups within groups, and Darwin says the hidden reason this works is that they share ancestors.
Naturalists look at deep likeness and not at outward looks. A whale looks like a fish, but it is placed with the mammals, because it breathes air and feeds its young with milk.
Darwin's own work on barnacles shows the point very well. Grown barnacles are fixed to rocks and look like shellfish, but their young swim freely like tiny crabs, which shows what they really are.
A human hand, a bat's wing, a horse's leg and a porpoise's flipper are all built from the same set of bones. Darwin asks what could be more curious than this pattern.
The same pattern appears in insects and in flowers as well. The biting jaws of a beetle and the long sucking tongue of a butterfly are made from the same basic parts, changed in shape.
The early embryos of fish, birds, reptiles and mammals look very much alike. The embryologist von Baer once said that he could not tell which was which, because he had forgotten the labels.
Darwin suggests that an embryo is a kind of dim picture of its ancestor. This would explain why the young of related animals look alike, even when the adults are very different.
Many animals carry small, useless parts called rudimentary organs. Unborn calves have teeth that never cut through the gum, and flightless birds have tiny wings that cannot lift them.
Darwin compares a rudimentary organ to a silent letter in a word. The letter is no longer sounded, but it remains in the spelling, where it offers a clue to the word's history.
Darwin sums up the chapter in a clear way. Descent with modification explains the groups, the matching limbs, the similar embryos and the leftover parts all at once.
In the last chapter, Darwin gathers the whole book together. He tells the reader that from beginning to end it has been one long argument.
Darwin argues that one idea explains many separate facts at once. Descent with modification through natural selection makes sense of fossils, geography, embryos and the habits of animals.
Darwin does not expect to convince everyone at once. Older naturalists are used to the old way of thinking, he says, so his hope lies with the younger ones who can weigh both sides.
In one short sentence, Darwin says that light will be thrown on the origin of mankind and its history. He says nothing more about people in this book.

Near the end, Darwin pictures a tangled bank covered with plants, with birds singing in the bushes and worms in the damp earth. All these different living things, he says, have been shaped by the same laws.

Those wolves that are a little swifter or slimmer than the rest will catch more deer, and so they will be the likeliest to survive and to raise pups of their own. Over many winters, he suggests, the whole pack might gradually become quicker and leaner than before.

Darwin heard that in the Catskill Mountains of the United States there were two varieties of wolf, which lived by quite different habits. One of them had a light, greyhound-like build and chased deer, while the other was bulkier, with shorter legs, and more often attacked the shepherd's flocks. This looked like the very process he had imagined, already under way in nature.

Darwin offers an example from the world of flowers, which shows the same principle at work. Suppose a plant makes a little sweet nectar at the base of its petals, so that insects seeking the nectar are dusted with pollen and carry it to other flowers of the same kind. Those plants with the largest supply of nectar would be visited most often, would set the most seed, and would leave the most descendants.

In a famous passage, Darwin describes natural selection as scrutinising, daily and hourly, throughout the world, every variation, even the slightest. It rejects what is bad and preserves what is good, working silently and insensibly, whenever and wherever the opportunity arises, to improve every living creature in relation to its conditions. We notice nothing, he says, until time has marked its long lapse, and by then the work has been done.

Darwin draws a sharp contrast between the breeder and nature, and the contrast is the heart of the matter. Man selects only for his own good, and he can act only on outside features that he can see. Nature selects only for the good of the creature that she tends, and she can work on every part of the body, with time on her side in quantities that no breeder could ever imagine.

Darwin adds a related process that he calls sexual selection, which depends not on the struggle to stay alive but on the struggle to find a mate. Stags fight one another, birds sing and display their feathers, and the winners leave more young to inherit their weapons or their beauty. The peacock's extravagant tail, a burden in many ways, may have grown by such a contest.

Darwin knew that the words natural selection might mislead, because they seem to suggest some being that makes a choice. He explains that by nature he means only the laws of the world as we find them, and that selection means only that some creatures survive and others do not. It does not make variations, he says, but only preserves the useful ones that arise.

Darwin stresses that the changes of natural selection are far too slow for any person to observe while they are going on. We see nothing of these slow changes in progress, he says, until the hand of time has marked the long lapse of ages. Looking at the world in one lifetime is like glancing at the hour hand of a clock and not noticing that it moves.

Darwin now explains why the descendants of one species tend to grow more and more different from each other over time. The more they differ, the less they compete for the same food and room, so a plot sown with several kinds of grass will yield more than a plot sown with one. A place can feed more life when its inhabitants live in many different ways at once.

Darwin pictures a meat-eating animal in a country where all the usual prey is already taken and the number of hunters cannot grow any more. Some of its descendants, driven to try something new, would begin to climb trees, or to hunt in water, or to eat a different diet, and the ones that did best would leave more young. Over thousands of generations they would grow quite different from their parents and from one another.

The one picture in the whole book is a large folding diagram, covered with branching lines that spread upward like the twigs of a tree. A row of letters from A to L along the bottom stands for the species of one big group, living in a single country. The lines above them show how, over a very long time, some species leave many new descendants, while others leave none.

In the diagram, the space between one horizontal line and the next stands for a thousand generations or more, so the whole picture covers a vast stretch of time. As the lines climb, most of them stop short, which means that most species leave no descendants, while a lucky few branch again and again. Darwin wanted his readers to see at a glance how rare success is, and how splendid it can be.

Darwin compares the whole history of life to a great tree, whose green and budding twigs represent the species living today. The twigs of former years stand for the long succession of species that have died out, and the great limbs and branches were once themselves only budding twigs. In this one picture he sums up the unity of life and the way in which it grows.

As new and better-adapted forms spread through a country, they take the place of the older forms that they most resemble, and these older forms become rare and finally disappear. Natural selection and extinction therefore go hand in hand, like two sides of one coin. It is the price that nature pays for every improvement, and the price is paid in every age of the world.

Darwin remembered a woodpecker that he had seen on the treeless plains of La Plata, where hardly a single tree grows. In every important part of its body it is a true woodpecker, with its toes, tail and tongue, yet it feeds on the ground and never climbs a tree. Such a bird shows how a creature's habits may change before its body does.

Darwin cautions that natural selection does not produce perfection, but only a fitness for each creature's own home and time. He points to New Zealand, where many native plants and animals have been beaten by newcomers from Europe, which were better suited to the struggle. A creature may be well adapted to its country and still not be the best that nature could produce.

Darwin considers the conditions that favour the rise of new forms, and he finds that a large area with many individuals offers the best supply of useful variations. Isolation helps too, because on an island or in a valley cut off from the rest a new form can keep its features without being swallowed back into the main population. Both things, size and separation, have their uses in the making of new species over time.

Darwin summarises his case as a chain of three links, none of which can reasonably be disputed. Living things vary, their useful variations tend to be inherited, and since far more are born than can live, those with the best-suited features will have the best chance of surviving. Together these facts make natural selection almost inevitable, he says, and the effect on living things must be large.

Chapter V opens with a frank and rather surprising confession from the author about the limits of his own knowledge. Darwin has sometimes spoken as though variations were due to chance, he says, but this is a wholly incorrect expression, which merely admits that we do not know the cause of each particular change. The word chance, in other words, is a label for his ignorance and not an explanation of anything.

Darwin tested the effects of use and disuse by weighing the bones of wild ducks against those of tame ducks. The tame birds, which walk about the yard much more than they fly, had lighter wing bones and heavier leg bones in proportion to the whole skeleton. Parts that are used grow stronger, it seems, and parts that are not used shrink.

Many domestic animals, including rabbits, pigs and some dogs, have ears that hang down, while their wild relatives rarely do. Darwin suggested that the reason might be disuse, because tame animals are seldom alarmed and therefore seldom need to prick their ears towards a sound. He was careful to present this as a likely explanation and not as a certainty.

In the dark caves of Europe and America, Darwin noted, there live beetles, fish and other animals that have lost their sight completely. He believed that the chief cause was disuse, for eyes are of no value in total darkness. It is also remarkable that each cave creature resembles the animals living outside the cave in the same part of the world.

Darwin noted that parts of an animal are linked together in ways that are quite unexpected, so that when one part changes, another follows. White cats with blue eyes are usually deaf, he observed, and pigeons with short beaks tend to have small feet, while hairless dogs often have imperfect teeth. He called this correlated variation, and he did not pretend to understand the causes.

Darwin noticed that features developed to an unusual degree, and especially the showy ornaments that distinguish the males of many species, tend to vary a great deal from one animal to another. This is useful to selection, since variable features offer more choice than steady ones. It may help to explain how such ornaments can change so quickly in a group of related species.

Darwin points to the dun-coloured horses of many different breeds, which sometimes show a dark stripe down the spine and faint bars across the legs. These marks, he reasons, are a return to the pattern of a striped ancestor, because the same marks are seen in wild asses and zebras, the horse's relatives. He calls this reversion, and it is another hint that all the horses descend from a common source.

Darwin observes that the features which distinguish one species from its close relatives tend to vary more than the features shared by the whole group. This is just what we should expect if the species had only recently begun to differ, since the recent changes would not yet have settled. Old features, shared by many species, have had much longer to become stable and fixed.

Darwin suggests that the growth of an animal follows a kind of economy, so that if a great deal is spent on building one part, less is left for another. He was borrowing the idea from earlier writers, and he saw that natural selection would also tend to reduce any part that proved useless, saving material for others. Nature, like a careful householder, does not like to waste anything that she could use elsewhere.

Darwin closes the chapter by returning to his ignorance, which he admits in the plainest words. Our ignorance of the laws of variation is profound, he writes, and in not one case out of a hundred can we pretend to say why some part has varied. Yet the fact of variation, whatever its cause, is not in doubt, and that is all his argument really needs.

Chapter VI is where Darwin turns critic of his own theory, and he does it with remarkable honesty. Long before the reader reaches this point, he says, a crowd of difficulties will have occurred to him, and some of them are so serious that for a long time they staggered him. He prefers to state them openly rather than to hope that nobody notices them.

The first difficulty is obvious, Darwin says: if species come from other species by fine steps, why do we not see in-between forms everywhere? His reply is that a variety living between two large groups would have to live on a narrow strip of country, with far fewer individuals than the groups on either side. It would therefore be easily beaten in the struggle, and so would soon vanish.

Darwin makes a startling admission about one of the most admired organs of the body. To suppose that the eye, with all its marvellous contrivances for adjusting focus and admitting light, could have been formed by natural selection seems, he freely confesses, absurd in the highest degree. It was not a very promising start to his defence of his own theory.

But reason comes to the rescue, Darwin says, because the living world contains a long series of eyes, from the simplest to the most perfect. The simplest consists of a nerve surrounded by dark colouring and covered with a clear skin, and from there the steps lead gradually to eyes with a lens. Since each step is useful to its owner, selection could have taken them one at a time.

Darwin then sets out a challenge to his own idea that few theorists would dare to make. If it could be demonstrated that any complex organ existed which could not possibly have been formed by numerous, successive, slight modifications, he writes, his theory would absolutely break down. Critics have proposed such organs ever since, and biologists have answered most of them with evidence of gradual steps.

Darwin considers the flying squirrel, which glides from tree to tree on a broad fold of skin stretched between its legs. Other kinds of squirrel have slightly flattened tails or slightly broader sides, and each of these small changes would help the animal when it leapt from branch to branch. A great change may grow, in other words, out of a long series of changes, each of which is useful.

Darwin notes that a part may do one job at first and later be turned to another, with little change in its shape. The swim bladder, which lets a fish float at the right depth, has the same ancient origin as the lungs by which other animals breathe air. Nature, it seems, is a thrifty craftsman that often prefers to adapt an old tool rather than invent a new one.

Darwin suggested that the long neck, legs and tongue of the giraffe suit it beautifully for browsing on the high branches of trees. In a season of famine, the tallest individuals, which could reach a little higher, would have the best chance of surviving. Scientists still debate the details of how the giraffe came to be so tall, but the principle is one that Darwin helped to teach us.

Darwin reminds the reader of a rule that older naturalists used to repeat in Latin, that nature does not make leaps. Natural selection can act only by taking advantage of slight successive variations, he says, and it must advance by the shortest and slowest steps. This is why the wonders of nature need long periods of time rather than sudden miracles.

Darwin closes the chapter with some very modest and careful words about the limits of knowledge. We are much too ignorant, he says, about the whole way of life of any one creature to say which slight changes would be of importance and which would not. The difficulties he has listed are real, but they are not final, and he believes that they should not outweigh the many facts that support his view.

Chapter VII turns from bodies to behaviour, and in particular to the instincts that make animals do clever things without any teacher. An instinctive action is one that many individuals perform in the same way, without experience and often without any idea of its purpose. Darwin argues that instincts are inherited and can vary, exactly as the shapes of bodies do.

Darwin finds proof that instincts can be altered by selection among tame animals, and he finds it in everyday places. A young pointer will stand and point at game the first time it is ever taken to the field, a sheepdog herds without training, and young tumbler pigeons somersault in the air before anyone has shown them how. Breeders chose these habits, he says, in exactly the way they chose beaks and tails.

Darwin argues that even the fear of human beings is an instinct that is acquired slowly, over many generations. On remote islands, such as the Galapagos, where people had seldom lived, the birds were so tame that he could almost touch them. Fear, it seems, must be learned afresh by each kind of animal, and the lesson takes a very long time.

Darwin considers the cuckoo, which lays its eggs in the nests of other birds and leaves the foster parents to raise its young. The newly hatched cuckoo, blind and naked, heaves its nest-mates over the edge so that it alone is fed. Darwin suggests that this strange habit may have arisen in small stages, each of which gave the cuckoo some small advantage.

Darwin describes one of the strangest instincts of all, that of the slave-making ants, which raid the nests of other ants and carry off their young. The stolen pupae hatch in the nest of the raiders and spend their lives doing its work, so that the masters depend on their captives. Darwin watched such a raid himself in southern England, and he never forgot the sight.

Darwin next admires the comb of the hive bee, a mass of tiny six-sided cells that fit together without wasting space. The shape stores the most honey with the least wax, and a mathematician could prove that no better pattern exists. Yet no bee has studied geometry, so the skill must somehow be written into its instincts.

To show how such a wonderful instinct might have grown, Darwin sets out a ladder of bees. The humble-bee stores honey in rough round pots, a tropical bee called Melipona builds neat round cells in a regular layer, and the hive bee has perfected the hexagonal comb. Each rung of this ladder is useful to its builders, and a path of small improvements seems to join them all.

Darwin explains that if round cells are made side by side at equal distances, the walls between them become flat and the cells take on a six-sided shape. A bee, therefore, needs no knowledge of geometry but only a few simple instincts, such as making round hollows of the right size and keeping them evenly spaced. Natural selection could improve these habits step by step, saving wax and thus saving honey.

One difficulty, Darwin confesses, at first appeared to him insuperable and actually fatal to his whole theory. The sterile workers of ants and bees often differ greatly from both their parents, yet they never have young of their own, so how could any useful feature be passed on? It seemed to be a case where natural selection could not possibly work at all.

Darwin's answer is that selection can act on the family as a whole, and not only on the individual. A breeder who has found an animal with excellent meat may return to the same family for more, even though the animal itself was killed, and in the same way nature favours colonies whose sterile workers are useful. Later biologists have developed this idea much further, but the idea began here with Darwin.

Chapter VIII faces a puzzle that seemed to many readers a serious objection to his theory. When two different species are crossed, their offspring, called hybrids, are usually unable to have young, whereas varieties of a single species cross freely, and this had long been taken as the mark of a true species. Darwin must now show that his theory can live comfortably with this puzzling fact.

The best-known hybrid of all is the mule, which is the offspring of a donkey and a horse. It is strong, patient and sure-footed, and farmers have prized it for centuries, but it is almost always unable to have young of its own. If this were true of all hybrids, species would seem to be separated by an unbreakable barrier.

Darwin draws on the work of two painstaking experimenters, Kolreuter and Gartner, who spent years crossing plants and recording every result. Their notes showed that sterility is not a single fixed barrier but comes in all degrees, from crosses that fail entirely to crosses that are almost as fertile as ordinary matings. A rule that fades away so gradually can hardly be a sharp mark of species.

Some of the results of these careful and patient experiments were very odd indeed, and puzzled the experimenters. The pollen of one species might fertilise a second species with ease, while the pollen of the second species could not fertilise the first at all, although exactly the same two plants were used each time. Such differences, Darwin concludes, must depend on tiny, hidden details of the reproductive system.

Darwin found that the ease with which two species can be crossed does not follow their outward resemblance. Species that look very different may cross quite readily, while others that are so similar that even experts hesitate to separate them may refuse to cross at all. The cause lies in a hidden part of their make-up that nobody could yet see.

Darwin reasons that natural selection can hardly have produced the sterility of hybrids, since it brings no advantage to any individual animal or plant. It must instead be a by-product, incidental to other differences in the reproductive systems of the parent species. It was not a special gift, in other words, given to keep species apart.

In the pigeon loft Darwin found the best evidence that varieties are fully fertile. Breeds as different as the fantail and the pouter mate freely and produce healthy young, and the same is true of dogs, cattle and chickens. This is in sharp contrast with the sterility of many true species, and it suggests that the two cases differ in degree.

Darwin does not hide the exceptions to his rule, because he believes that the whole truth strengthens his argument. There are a few cases in which two varieties of the same plant are partly infertile with each other, and these show that the line between varieties and true species is not perfectly sharp. Everywhere in nature, he reminds us, one group fades into another, and sterility is no different.

Today biologists know that the infertility of hybrids arises from differences in the genes and chromosomes that the two parents carry, a discovery that was still far in the future when Darwin wrote. Modern research largely supports his view that this infertility is a by-product of other differences between species. It was not a barrier that was designed to keep species apart from one another.

Darwin closes the chapter with quiet confidence in the strength of his argument and in the facts he has set out. The fertility and sterility of crosses, he says, are not a special endowment that separates species from varieties, but are incidental to differences in the reproductive systems of the parents. Hybrids, which looked like a wall in the path of his theory, turn out to be only a stone in the road.

Chapter IX takes up what Darwin regarded as the most obvious and gravest objection to his theory. If species have changed slowly, the rocks ought to be full of the in-between forms that link one kind to another, and yet they are not. His answer, which he develops carefully, is that the geological record is far more imperfect than most people suppose.

Darwin compares the record of the rocks to a history of the world that has been imperfectly kept and written in a changing dialect. Of this history we possess only the last volume, he says, relating to just two or three countries. Of that volume, only here and there a short chapter has been preserved, and of each page only here and there a few lines.

Darwin insists that his argument depends upon an almost unimaginable length of time for its success. A reader who cannot feel the vastness of the ages, he says, should study Lyell's great work on geology and, if he is still unconvinced, put this volume down at once. It was a bold challenge, but Darwin knew that his whole case would fail without it.

To give his readers a sense of the vast spans of time, Darwin attempted to calculate how long the rain and the sea had taken to wear away the Weald, a district of south-east England. He arrived at a figure of hundreds of millions of years, though he later withdrew it when critics pointed out how uncertain the method was. The lesson was that geological time is very long, whatever the exact number turns out to be.

Darwin explains that fossils form only under special conditions, and that most dead creatures leave no trace at all. The body must be buried quickly in mud or sand, usually under water, before it can rot or be eaten, and then it must lie undisturbed for an immense length of time. The wonder is not how few fossils there are but how many have survived.

Land animals are rare as fossils, Darwin points out, because they usually die on the surface, where scavengers and weather destroy their bones before anything can bury them. Soft-bodied creatures, such as worms and jellyfish, almost never leave any trace at all. What we see in the rocks is therefore a very small and rather biased sample of the life of the past.

Layers of rock pile up in separate patches at separate times, and many of them are afterwards lifted, worn away and lost. For this reason the record of the rocks is full of gaps, some of which, Darwin suspects, represent much longer periods than the layers that remain. It is as though a film of the past had survived only as a handful of scattered frames.

Soon after Darwin's book appeared, workmen in a German quarry uncovered the fossil of Archaeopteryx, a creature about 150 million years old. It had the wings and feathers of a bird, yet it also had teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail like a reptile. Darwin added it to later editions of his book as just the sort of in-between form that his theory led him to expect.

Some groups of animals seem to appear in the rocks all at once, with no ancestors in the layers below. Darwin replies that they may have lived and changed for ages in some other region, in earlier layers that are lost or not yet found, and then migrated to the place where we see them. The suddenness, in other words, may belong to the record and not to nature itself.

Darwin concludes that the gaps in the geological record are precisely what his theory would lead us to expect, given the rarity of fossils and the immensity of time. They are therefore no proof against his argument, but only a reminder of how much of the history of life has been lost. What the rocks do preserve, as the next chapter shows, tells the same story.

Chapter X looks at how fossils are arranged in time, from the oldest rocks at the bottom to the youngest at the top. New species appear slowly and one by one, Darwin says, and a species that has once vanished from the Earth never returns. This pattern is just what we should expect if living things are bound together by descent.

Darwin argues that species seldom vanish all at once from the face of the world. They first become rare, then rarer still, and at last disappear as new and better-fitted rivals spread through the country, so that extinction is the slow companion of change. We should not be surprised at the end of a species, he says, any more than at the death of an individual.

In South America, Darwin himself had found a horse's tooth buried in the rocks beside the bones of giant extinct animals. Horses had therefore lived there long ago and then died out, and yet the horses brought by Europeans multiplied wonderfully on the same plains. The puzzle taught him that extinction cannot always be blamed on a country becoming unsuitable.

Darwin noted a steady pattern in the fossils, which is that the older the layer of rock, the more its creatures differ from those that live today. Layers that lie close together in age contain fossils that closely resemble one another, as the generations of a family do. It is exactly the pattern that slow and continuous change would produce over time.

In South America, Darwin observed, the giant fossil animals, such as great armour-plated creatures like armadillos and huge ground sloths, are plainly related to the smaller animals still living on the same continent. He called it a wonderful relationship, in the same continent, between the dead and the living. Descent from common ancestors, he argued, would explain it, whereas separate creations would not.

The same rule, Darwin points out, applies to Australia, where the bones found in caves belong to pouched animals closely related to the kangaroos and other marsupials of the present day. It seems that each land has long had its own families of creatures, and that its past and its present are linked together by descent. Such a link between old and new is just what descent with modification would lead us to predict.

Darwin notes that many fossils stand between the living groups, and so partly fill the wide gaps that separate one family or order of animals from another. If we could see all the creatures of the past, the divisions between groups of living things would seem much less sharp than they do at present. The living world is only the surviving tips of a far larger tree, most of whose branches have been lost.

Darwin observes that a few creatures, such as the shellfish called Lingula, have remained almost unchanged since the oldest fossil-bearing rocks. Nature does not demand that every species should change at the same rate, he explains, and if conditions stay the same, a well-fitted form may last for ages. Change happens when it is useful, and not because of some law that forces it.

Darwin openly admits one real puzzle, which is that the oldest rocks containing fossils already hold quite complex animals, with no sign of ancestors in the layers below. He confesses that he cannot give a satisfactory answer, and that the case might fairly be urged as an argument against his views. Since his day, fossils of simpler life have been found in much older rocks, which has eased the difficulty.

Darwin concludes that, imperfect as the fossil record is, it agrees with his theory in the way that matters most. Fossils follow the pattern of a family tree, with the older kinds resembling the ancestors of the newer, and the history of life appears to be a long story of descent with modification. For Darwin, the dead and the living belong to a single great family, and the rocks are its album.

Chapters XI and XII turn to geography, and they begin with a real puzzle in nature. Lands with very similar climates, such as the hot forests of Africa and South America, are often home to very different animals and plants, which means that climate alone cannot explain where a creature lives. Something about the history of each region must matter as well, and Darwin sets out to find what it is.

Darwin points out that great barriers, such as wide seas, deserts and mountain ranges, mark the boundaries between regions, and that the creatures on the two sides tend to be different. The fish and shellfish of the seas on the two sides of the narrow Isthmus of Panama, for instance, are mostly of different kinds. Those that can cross a barrier are common, while those that cannot remain apart.

Darwin supposes that each species first appeared in one particular place, and then spread outward from there for as far as barriers and rivals would permit. If this is true, living things must possess many ways of crossing the sea and other obstacles, and that is where his experiments begin. They were simple, inexpensive and surprisingly instructive for anyone who cares about how life travels.

Darwin soaked the seeds of dozens of different plants in bowls of salt water, some for weeks, to see whether they could survive a long sea journey. To his delight, many of them sprouted when he planted them afterwards, which showed that a floating seed might well cross an ocean on the currents. It was a small experiment with large consequences for the study of how plants are spread across the world.

Darwin found another way in which plants might travel, which was on the muddy feet and feathers of birds. From a few spoonfuls of mud taken from the edge of a pond, he raised a surprising number of different plants, which proved that wading birds could carry them from one pond to another. The seeds had moved without any plan, without any help, and without any passport at all.

Darwin describes the Glacial period, when great sheets of ice spread over the northern lands and drove plants and animals of cold regions far to the south. When the climate warmed again, those creatures retreated either northward or up the mountains, which explains why the same kinds of alpine plants grow on distant mountain tops and also in the Arctic. In the cold ages, the Alps and the far north had shared one flora.

Darwin notes that remote islands in the middle of the ocean hold few kinds of living things, and that whole groups are missing from them. There are no frogs, toads or newts, whose eggs and skin cannot bear salt water, and no land mammals except bats, which are able to fly there. The empty places on the list tell us as much as the full ones do.

Darwin visited both the Galapagos Islands and the Cape Verde Islands, which are alike in their volcanic rocks and in their warm dry climate. Yet the living things of the Galapagos resemble those of South America, while those of the Cape Verde Islands resemble those of Africa. Climate and soil could not explain the likeness, but the sea currents and the nearness of each mainland could.

Within the Galapagos group, Darwin saw, each island has its own forms of mockingbird, tortoise and other creatures, which are close relatives of one another and of the animals of nearby South America. Many of them live nowhere else on Earth, not even on the next island. Here, in the very islands that had puzzled him on the Beagle, the pattern of descent from a few early arrivals was plain.

On windy islands such as Madeira, a good number of the beetles have lost the power of flight, a fact that the naturalist Wollaston had recorded with care. Darwin explained it by natural selection, since those beetles that flew were often blown out to sea, while the wingless ones stayed safe at home and left more young. A feature that is useful on a continent may be a danger on an island.

Chapter XIII begins with the way naturalists classify living things into groups nested within larger groups, like a set of boxes. Darwin says that the hidden bond which has been sought under the name of the natural system is nothing but descent from common ancestors. The family tree of life, in other words, is the real reason why the groups exist at all.

Naturalists have learned to look at deep likeness rather than outward appearance when they classify living things. A whale is shaped like a fish and lives in the sea, yet it breathes air, keeps its young warm and feeds them on milk, and so it is placed among the mammals. Such deep likenesses, Darwin argues, are the marks of descent from a common ancestor.

Darwin's own work on barnacles gave him a vivid example of this principle at work. Grown barnacles are fixed to rocks and look at first like shellfish, but their young swim freely about and are plainly of the same type as crabs and other crustaceans. The truth about their family was written in their childhood, and Darwin had been among the first people to read it.

What could be more curious, Darwin asks, than that the hand of a man, the wing of a bat, the leg of a horse and the flipper of a porpoise are all built on the same pattern? The same bones appear in the same order in each of them, though their uses are completely different. The simplest explanation is that all these animals have inherited their limbs from a common ancestor.

The same pattern turns up again and again, Darwin shows, in many different places. The biting jaws of a beetle and the long sucking tongue of a butterfly are built from the same basic parts, simply bent to different uses. In the same way the petals and other parts of a flower are altered leaves, and nature seems to prefer remodelling old parts to making new ones from nothing.

When Darwin looked at the very young embryos of animals with backbones, he found that fish, birds, reptiles and mammals look remarkably alike. The great embryologist Karl Ernst von Baer admitted that he had two small embryos in spirits, which he had forgotten to label, and that he could no longer say to which class they belonged. They might be lizards, small birds or very young mammals, he said, and he could not tell.

Darwin reasons that an embryo is a kind of picture, more or less obscured, of the ancestor of the whole group to which it belongs. This would explain why the young of related animals resemble one another so closely, even when the adults have grown to be very different. The beginning of an animal's life keeps a faint memory of its family's past.

Many animals carry small and apparently useless parts, which Darwin calls rudimentary organs, and which are found everywhere in nature. Unborn calves have teeth in the upper jaw that never cut through the gum, snakes may have tiny traces of hip bones, and flightless birds have wings far too small to lift them. Such features are puzzling if each animal was designed fresh, but easy to understand as leftovers from ancestors.

Darwin offers a charming and memorable comparison for these leftover parts of the body. A rudimentary organ, he says, is like a letter in a word that is still kept in the spelling although it is no longer sounded, and that serves as a clue to the word's origin. The silent letters of an animal's body can be read in the same way, as clues to its family history.

Darwin sums up the chapter by pointing out how much a single idea explains. Descent with modification accounts for classification, for the matching limbs of different animals, for the likeness of embryos and for the strange leftover organs, all at the same time. A theory that makes sense of so many separate facts, he says, deserves to be taken seriously.

In the final chapter, Darwin gathers the whole book together and reminds the reader what he has been trying to do. From beginning to end, he says, the volume has been one long argument, in which each fact supports the next. He asks the reader to judge it as a whole and not point by point.

Darwin argues that a single idea, descent with modification through natural selection, makes sense of many separate facts that would otherwise remain unconnected. It explains the fossils in the rocks, the plants and animals of islands, the likeness of embryos and the leftover organs of the body. A good theory, he suggests, is one that ties together many things that were previously a mystery.

Darwin does not expect to win over everyone, and he says as much without bitterness. Older naturalists, whose minds are full of facts seen from the old point of view, are unlikely to change. His hope lies with the young and rising naturalists, who will be able to weigh both sides of the question fairly, and he had the patience to wait for a new generation.

Tucked away in the last pages is a single short sentence in which Darwin promises that light will be thrown on the origin of man and his history. He says nothing more on the subject in this book, for he knew how strongly people would react. Twelve years later he wrote a whole book about it, called The Descent of Man.

In his closing paragraph Darwin invites us to look at a tangled bank, thickly covered with many kinds of plants, with birds singing in the bushes, insects flitting about and worms crawling through the damp earth. These elaborate forms, so different from one another and yet so dependent on each other, have all been produced by laws acting around us. It is a picture that is at once ordinary and astonishing, and Darwin leaves it for the reader to ponder.

Darwin ends the book on a note of wonder, and chooses his last words with great care. There is grandeur in this view of life, he writes, for from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved. The word evolved, which appears here only at the very end of the book, was to become the name of his whole idea.

The first printing of about 1,250 copies was bought up by booksellers almost at once, and the publisher soon had to prepare more. A second edition of about 3,000 copies appeared in January 1860, and the book became the subject of passionate argument in newspapers, lecture halls and drawing rooms. Darwin, who was still unwell, read the reviews with a mixture of pride and anxiety.

The scientist Thomas Huxley read the book at once, said that he felt foolish for not having thought of the idea himself, and became its chief defender. In June 1860, at a meeting in Oxford, he argued about it with Bishop Samuel Wilberforce in front of a large crowd, although Darwin himself was not there. Accounts of what was actually said differ, and the story has grown with each telling.

Darwin spent the rest of his life improving the book through six editions and writing more, on orchids, on earthworms and on the descent of humankind. He died at Down House on 19 April 1882, and the nation honoured him with a burial in Westminster Abbey, close to the grave of Isaac Newton. Wallace was among those who carried his coffin to its resting place that day.

Later discoveries, above all in the science of genes, which Darwin knew nothing about, have corrected and enriched his ideas in many details. Yet the core of his argument, that living things are related by descent and shaped by natural selection, is still the foundation of modern biology. Look again at the tangled bank outside your window, and you will see what Darwin saw.
